bodyHtml:
To give your AI agent a body today, you build it a small gadget: a screen, a push-to-talk button, a speaker, a camera or a Linux box it can use. The most direct route is Meta's Muse Gadgets SDK, which turns off-the-shelf ESP32 boards and Raspberry Pi computers into devices for Muse, Meta's personal AI agent. A pocket stick you can talk to costs $21.50, and setup fits in an afternoon. This guide covers what a body can do, the main options, the real costs and how hackshop plans it with you.

Quick answer

Pick a board Muse supports, flash Meta's open-source firmware over a USB data cable, and pair it in the Muse app under Settings > Devices with Developer mode on. The M5Stack StickS3 ($21.50) is the cheapest board in hackshop's catalog with a screen, mic and speaker. The round Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C ($39.99 to $41.99) is the best desk object. A Raspberry Pi gives Muse a shell on a Linux computer instead.

What it means to give your AI agent a body

Your agent already has a brain and, with Muse, a computer of its own. Meta announced Muse on September 8, 2026 as a personal AI agent for iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp, rolling out in the US. Each user gets Muse Secure VM, which Meta calls "a persistent, isolated Linux computer with a full browser". What the agent lacks is a presence in your room.

A body fills that gap. Meta announced Muse Gadgets on October 2, 2026, and its own wording is the best definition: "Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself. Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators…" There are two kinds of body today:

  • ESP32 gadgets. Small boards where you can "throw in a screen to show images, add audio in and out, or wire up other sensors."
  • Linux gadgets. A spare Raspberry Pi or Linux box that Muse can run commands on, for sysadmin chores or a Home Assistant setup.

Keep expectations grounded. The thinking still happens in Muse, not on the board. Push-to-talk sends a voice note, Muse transcribes it and answers in text, and boards with a screen show the answer as captions. Spoken replies need a text-to-speech service you hook up yourself. If you use Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor, those agents can plan and flash the build for you, but the finished gadget pairs with Muse.

The main options, compared

Meta's firmware lists 24 supported ESP32 boards, plus Raspberry Pi and other Linux machines with Bluetooth LE. These are the ones most people start with. Prices are from each seller's US page.

The ESP32 boards come in two tiers. Full UI boards show an avatar and offer push-to-talk and settings on the device. Status boards show Muse's state on a light or a simple screen. Meta's suggested first board, the Espressif ESP32-C5-DevKitC-1, is a status board: a light and a button. See every board side by side on the Muse board comparison.

Meta also makes hardware you don't build. Muse Home Link connects Muse to your home Wi-Fi and is "free with an active Muse subscription in the United States only, limit one per subscriber." A TV stick is listed as coming soon, and Meta previewed a pocket device called Muse Charm at Connect 2026 with no price yet. If you want zero tinkering, those may suit you better.

What it costs

The board is most of the bill. Add a USB-C cable that carries data (hackshop's plans budget about $8) and, for bare boards, a stand. With seller prices plus that cable, typical totals are:

  • M5Stack StickS3: about $30
  • AIPI Lite: about $44. It ships with a battery but no cable or power adapter.
  • Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C: about $48
  • Seeed SenseCAP Watcher: about $69

Raspberry Pi prices have climbed. Raspberry Pi has raised them several times since late 2025 "to offset the recent unprecedented rise in the cost of LPDDR4 memory", so a Pi 5 now lists at $45 (1GB), $110 (4GB) or $175 (8GB). The $15 Pi Zero 2 W is slow but enough for shell and file commands. A Pi also needs a power supply and a microSD card, and the Pi 5 wants 5 V at 5 A over USB-C.

Muse itself is "free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more," in Meta's words; the announcement gives no plan prices. Time is the other cost. Hackshop's build pages estimate one to three hours of setup for most boards, and installing the toolchain is the slow part. Budget for the odd mistake, too. Meta's own page warns, "Side effects of tinkering may include bricked boards, voided warranties, brownouts, or bankruptcies."

How hackshop plans your build

Hackshop is a free, open-source planner for agent bodies, starting with Muse. It does four jobs:

  1. Picks the board. Describe what you want in the planner and set a budget. It shortlists boards that can do the job and says what each one can't do.
  2. Lists the parts. Each build has a shopping list with seller and Amazon links, and the store page collects every board and part. Hackshop doesn't sell hardware.
  3. Writes the steps. Each build page covers flashing, pairing, a printable stand where one exists, and a checklist that saves to My builds. The StickS3 build is a good example.
  4. Briefs your agent. Every build includes a brief your coding agent can follow, and hackshop runs an MCP server so Claude, Codex or Cursor can plan the build themselves.

Whoever drives, the rule is the same: nothing gets bought without your OK. Your agent shows you the items and total first, and where a store doesn't allow automated checkout, it hands you the link.

Rules and risks to know first

  • Personal use only. The firmware is Apache 2.0, but the SDK token every gadget needs is "for personal, non-commercial use". A token links to 50 devices at most, and you can't put one in a device you sell or list publicly.
  • No guarantees. Meta says the SDK and tokens "are not a supported product and not a developer platform. They may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time".
  • Pair on a network you trust. Pairing "has no manufacturer verification and can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack." Meta also strongly recommends NVS encryption, which protects the Wi-Fi credentials and tokens stored on the board.
  • Linux gadgets act as you. On a Pi, "If it can use sudo, so can Muse." Run it under an account with only the access you mean to give.
  • Cameras and mics live in your home. Point a camera at one job, like a 3D printer, not at people.

Every board on hackshop also carries a difficulty rating, like a ski run: green circle for Beginner (no tools), blue square for Intermediate (extra steps such as a backup before flashing), and black diamond for Expert (needs a pro, or buy something finished). You can also look inside each board in 3D before you buy, and vote on build ideas other people want.

Questions people ask

Can I give Claude or ChatGPT a body this way?

Not directly. Muse Gadgets pair with Muse, Meta's agent, using an SDK token from your Muse account. Claude, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents can still do the work: Meta's repo includes AGENTS.md files, and any agent that reads them can build and flash the firmware for you.

Do I need electronics experience?

No. For the boards in this guide, you don't wire anything. You plug the board into a Mac or Linux computer with a USB data cable, flash the firmware and pair it in the Muse app. The fiddly parts are installing the exact ESP-IDF version (6.0.1) and finding the right serial port.

Will my agent's body talk back?

Muse replies in text, and boards with a screen show the reply as captions. Boards with a speaker can speak replies if you connect a text-to-speech service; the SDK marks where to hook it in.

What is the cheapest way to give my AI agent a body?

The M5Stack StickS3 at $21.50 is the cheapest board in hackshop's catalog with a screen, mic, speaker and battery. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W costs $15 but has no screen or speaker; it gives Muse a Linux shell instead.

Can I sell the gadgets I build?

Not with a Muse token inside. The SDK terms bar putting a token in any device you sell, advertise or list publicly, and other distribution needs Meta's written permission.

Your AI agent needs a physical device when its job happens away from your screen: a status you want to glance at, a question you want to ask with your hands full, a camera watching one thing, or a computer it should look after. A device gives it a fixed place and a few senses. If you mostly chat with your agent at a desk, you probably don't need one. Here are the good reasons, the honest reasons to skip it, and how to choose.

Quick answer

Get a device if you want ambient status on a desk or wall, push-to-talk without reaching for your phone, a camera Muse can check on request, or a Raspberry Pi that runs chores. Skip it if your agent use is long chats and writing, if you don't want another mic at home, or if you need a supported product rather than an as-is SDK. A pocket gadget you can talk to, the M5Stack StickS3, costs $21.50.

What a physical device adds to an AI agent

An agent like Muse already runs wherever you carry a screen. Meta's agent works on iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp, and Meta says its new glasses connect to it too. What it can't do from there is stay in one place. It can't sit on your desk showing what it's working on, hang by the door, or keep an eye on your 3D printer.

A device fixes that. Meta's Muse Gadgets SDK, announced October 2, 2026, turns off-the-shelf ESP32 boards and Raspberry Pi computers into gadgets, so Muse can use "your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators". The board doesn't run the AI. Push-to-talk sends a voice note, Muse transcribes it and answers in text, and boards with a screen show the reply as captions.

Why your AI agent needs a physical device: five reasons

1. Ambient presence and glanceable status

A screen that stays on tells you what the agent is doing without a tap. The round Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C shows an avatar on your desk for $39.99 to $41.99. On a wall, the Seeed reTerminal E1001 shows status text and black-and-white images on 7.5-inch e-paper that refreshes in "a second or two." The color E1002 takes about 30 seconds and flashes, so save it for things that change slowly, like a daily calendar.

2. Voice without your phone

Pressing a button is faster than picking up a phone, opening an app and typing. The M5Stack StickS3 ($21.50) is a pocket push-to-talk remote with a mic, a 1 W speaker and a 250 mAh battery. The Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition ($69) does the same from a shelf, with its center button as push-to-talk. It has no screen, so its replies show up in the Muse app.

3. Camera context

The Seeed SenseCAP Watcher ($60.99) has a camera, and Muse can ask it for a photo. Point it at a 3D printer and ask whether the print failed. A camera in your home is a real privacy exposure, so aim it at one job and keep people out of frame.

4. Sensing the room

Some boards read the room for the agent. The Seeed SenseCAP Indicator in its D1S and D1Pro versions has air sensors that Muse can read when you ask.

5. Hands on a real computer

A spare Raspberry Pi becomes a place where Muse can run shell commands and read or write files. Meta pitches it for "sysadmin chores or your Home Assistant setup." The $15 Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is enough for shell and file work. The catch, in Meta's words: "If it can use sudo, so can Muse."

Desk, kitchen and wall: where a device earns its place

In the kitchen, a prompt like "Add milk to the grocery list" is the whole point: one press, one sentence, done. At the desk, the value is the glance. You see that the agent is busy, finished or waiting on you without switching windows. For a fridge calendar, see the e-paper family calendar guide. If you're unsure where yours would go, read where your AI agent should live.

When you don't need one

A device is a bad buy in plenty of cases. Be honest with yourself about these:

  • Your agent work is long-form. Research, writing and planning belong on a big screen with a keyboard. A 1.14-inch screen won't help.
  • You want spoken conversation out of the box. Muse replies in text. Spoken replies need a text-to-speech service you connect yourself.
  • You don't want another mic or camera at home. That's a fair call. Voice boards use push-to-talk, but a camera board is still a camera.
  • You need something supported. Meta says the SDK and tokens "are not a supported product" and "may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time."
  • You'd rather not build. Meta's Muse Home Link is free with an active Muse subscription in the US, and Meta previewed a pocket device, Muse Charm, with no price announced yet.
  • You want to sell what you make. Muse SDK tokens are for personal, non-commercial use. Selling a Muse-connected device needs Meta's written permission.

A quick test before you buy

  1. Name three things you'd say to it in a normal week. If you can't, wait.
  2. Pick the spot. A device you have to go and fetch is just a phone with fewer features.
  3. Decide how you'll talk to it. Read push-to-talk vs always-listening devices if you're unsure.
  4. Set a budget, then let the Muse board picker match a board to it.

If all four have answers, a gadget in the $22 to $70 range is a small bet with a clear job. If not, keep using the app and revisit when a use comes up twice.

bodyHtml:
You can build an AI agent body in an afternoon once the parts are on your desk. Pick a board that Meta's Muse firmware supports, flash it from a Mac or Linux computer over a USB data cable, pair it in the Muse app, and put it where you'll use it. Hackshop's build pages estimate one to three hours of setup for most boards, and a typical build costs about $30 to $70 with a cable. The ordering happens a few days before.

Quick answer

Order a supported board and a USB-C data cable. Get an SDK token at gadgets.muse.ai, install ESP-IDF v6.0.1, set the token, then build and flash. In the Muse app, turn on Developer mode under Settings > Devices, add the MuseGadget device and press its button when the light breathes blue. Green means connected. The M5Stack StickS3 ($21.50) is the cheapest board here you can talk to, and the round Waveshare display ($39.99 to $41.99) is the nicest desk object.

What you need before you start

  • A supported board. Step 1 helps you pick one.
  • "A USB cable that carries data, not just power." Meta lists this as a requirement. A charge-only cable can't flash a board, and it's an easy mistake to make.
  • A computer running macOS or Linux. Windows isn't on Meta's list for the ESP32 SDK.
  • An SDK token from gadgets.muse.ai, under Account > SDK tokens. Every gadget needs one to pair.
  • The Muse app on an iPhone or Android phone.
  • Optional: a printed stand for bare boards.

Step 1: Pick a board

Choose by where it will live and how you'll talk to it. For a first build, these five cover most needs:

BoardGood forPriceFirst-flash notes
Espressif ESP32-C5-DevKitC-1Easiest first flash; status light onlyLaunched at $15 in 2025Works as-is with its status light and BOOT button
M5Stack StickS3Pocket push-to-talk$21.50Ships with UiFlow2, which turns off USB serial, and has no BOOT button. Back up its 8 MB flash, then follow the one-time steps in Meta's notes.
AIPI LitePalm-size buddy with a battery$35.99No USB-C cable or power adapter in the box
Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75CRound desk display$39.99 to $41.99Comes in an aluminum case; the higher price appears to be the version with a battery
Seeed SenseCAP WatcherA camera Muse can use$60.99Back up its factory data first; a flash shows nothing for about three minutes

If you want a face on your desk, take the Waveshare. If you want the cheapest board you can talk to, take the StickS3 and allow extra time for its first flash. If you only want to prove the whole chain works, the C5 DevKitC-1 is Meta's suggested quickest start. Save the Watcher for your second build.

Step 2: Order the parts

Every board and part is on the hackshop store page with seller and Amazon links. Hackshop doesn't sell hardware, and nothing gets bought without your OK. Add a USB-C data cable (hackshop budgets about $8) and the totals land here:

  • StickS3 build: about $30
  • AIPI Lite build: about $44
  • Waveshare round display build: about $48
  • SenseCAP Watcher build: about $69

Order a few days ahead, since shipping times vary by seller. For a stand, print hackshop's STL file yourself or order a print from a library or service.

Step 3: Flash the Muse firmware

  1. Get your token. Create one at gadgets.muse.ai under Account > SDK tokens. Keep it out of public repos and posts.
  2. Install ESP-IDF v6.0.1 exactly. Meta's README says "Other versions aren't supported." Espressif's docs now default to v6.1, so don't just grab the latest.
  3. Get the SDK. Clone facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk from GitHub and work in its esp32 folder.
  4. Set the token. Run idf.py menuconfig and enter it under ESP32 Device SDK.
  5. Build and flash. Build with your board's command from its build page, such as tools/muse/board.sh build sticks3, then run idf.py -p PORT flash monitor.

PORT is your board's serial port. On a Mac it looks like /dev/cu.usb*; on Linux, /dev/ttyACM* or /dev/ttyUSB*. The ESP32 port finder helps you pick the right one. If flashing can't connect, Meta's advice is to "hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT, and try again." On Linux, add yourself to the dialout group and log back in.

Prefer not to type commands? Meta's repo includes AGENTS.md files, and in its words, "Any agent that reads AGENTS.md can build and flash from this repository." Meta's own Muse Code works too. See how to let your agent plan and build it.

Step 4: Pair it with the Muse app

After a good flash, the status light breathes orange, which means it's ready for setup. On boards with a screen, the edge bars or avatar show the same colors.

  1. In the Muse app, turn on Settings > Devices > Developer mode.
  2. Tap Add Device (the + icon) and pick the device whose name starts with MuseGadget.
  3. When the light breathes blue, press the board's button to confirm it's you.
  4. Wait for green. That means Muse is connected.

Yellow blinking means reconnecting, purple means not paired, and red blinking means something went wrong, so check the log. Hold the button for 5 seconds to reset and start over. Pair on a network you trust, because pairing "can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack." Reflashing later keeps your pairing and Wi-Fi settings.

Step 5: Place it and say hello

Put the board on its stand or shelf, route the cable so it doesn't lift the board, and check that you can reach the buttons. Then try a first prompt from its build page, such as "(Hold to talk) Add milk to the grocery list." Muse answers in text, shown as captions on boards with a screen. Want shorter replies? Ask for them in the message: "Answer in one sentence."

One setting is worth a minute: Meta strongly recommends turning on NVS encryption, because your Wi-Fi credentials and device tokens sit in flash where anyone holding the board could read them.

How long it takes to build an AI agent body, and what it costs

Hackshop's estimates are one to two hours for the StickS3 and one to three hours for most other boards, counted from when the parts arrive. Writing the firmware takes seconds; Espressif's sample log shows about 3 seconds of write time. The slow parts are installing the toolchain and the first build. Two exceptions run longer: a SenseCAP Watcher flash "shows nothing for about three minutes," and putting your own avatar on a board "takes several minutes, mostly waiting for Muse."

Costs run about $30 to $70 for an ESP32 build with a cable. Muse itself is free for most uses, with paid plans that Meta's announcement doesn't price. Ready to go? Start a build to save the parts list and checklist.

Questions people ask

Can I build an AI agent body on Windows?

Meta's ESP32 SDK lists a computer running macOS or Linux as a requirement, and Windows isn't on that list. Use a Mac or a Linux machine for flashing.

My board doesn't show up. What now?

Swap to a cable you know carries data, try another USB port and check the port name. On Linux, add yourself to the dialout group and log back in. If flashing still fails, hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT and retry.

Will reflashing erase my pairing?

No. Reflashing keeps your pairing and Wi-Fi settings. Only an erase-flash wipes them.

Can my coding agent do the whole build?

Most of it. Any agent that reads the repo's AGENTS.md can build and flash. Approving and buying parts, and pairing in the Muse app on your phone, stay with you.

bodyHtml:
The hackshop MCP server lets a coding agent such as Claude, Codex or Cursor plan its own physical body. It asks you a few questions, shortlists boards for Meta's Muse Gadgets SDK, builds the parts list and walks you through flashing and pairing. You add it once, as a remote server at https://www.hackshop.dev/mcp or locally with npx -y hackshop-mcp. It never buys anything without your OK.

Quick answer

Add https://www.hackshop.dev/mcp to your agent as a remote MCP server, then ask it to plan a body for itself. It uses four tools: intake_gadget for the few questions to ask you, plan_gadget to shortlist boards, get_build_plan for parts, steps and an agent brief, and assess_hackability to check a device you already own. Nothing gets bought until you approve the exact items and total.

What the hackshop MCP server does

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is "an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems." Its own docs compare it to "a USB-C port for AI applications." Anthropic introduced it in November 2024, and it now sits with the Agentic AI Foundation, a fund under the Linux Foundation.

Hackshop's server gives your agent hardware knowledge it doesn't have on its own: which boards Muse supports, what each can do, what it costs, and the exact steps to flash and pair it. Besides its tools, it offers a prompt called plan-muse-gadget that walks an agent through intake, planning, shopping-list approval and assembly, plus a resource that lists every Muse board.

The tools need no API key and no account. plan_gadget doesn't call a language model or the network, so the same request gives the same picks every time.

How to connect the hackshop MCP server

Claude Code, one command:

claude mcp add --transport http hackshop https://www.hackshop.dev/mcp

Cursor or Claude Desktop, running the npm package locally. In Cursor this goes in ~/.cursor/mcp.json or a project's .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "hackshop": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "hackshop-mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Codex, in ~/.codex/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.hackshop]
url = "https://www.hackshop.dev/mcp"

ChatGPT, or any agent without MCP: paste the prompt from the hackshop homepage. It points the agent at hackshop's agent instructions, which carry the same rules.

Two notes on the npm package. It sends anonymous usage telemetry (tool names and timings only) by default; set HACKSHOP_TELEMETRY=0 to turn it off. It also adds propose_hardware and simulate_assembly for broader hardware ideas and robot simulation. This guide sticks to the tools both versions share.

The tools and what they return

ToolYou give itIt returns
intake_gadgetNothingThe four intake questions (where it lives, how you'll use it, whether it should sense the room, budget), why each matters and how the answers map to plan_gadget
plan_gadgetYour idea in plain words and your intake answers, plus an optional budget, size (pocket, desk, wall or hidden), needs (voice, screen, camera, e-ink, battery and more) and boards you already ownThree ranked picks by default, up to five, each with why it fits, its gaps, price, difficulty level and build page; warnings and intake questions; the Muse SDK terms; next steps
get_build_planOne device id, such as aipi-liteParts and a shopping list with a purchase policy, numbered steps with exact commands, assembly steps, first prompts to try, caveats and a Markdown brief for your agent

get_build_plan also links the human page for the same build, such as the AIPI Lite build, so you can follow along and save progress to My builds.

What a planning session looks like

Try a prompt like this:

Use the hackshop MCP to plan a body for yourself. I want something on my desk I can talk to, under $50. Ask me up to four questions first. Then show me one parts list with links and the total. Don't buy anything.

Hackshop's instructions tell agents to "ask at most 4 questions about size, interaction, sensing and budget." A test run of plan_gadget on October 5, 2026, with the vague idea "something on my desk for my agent" and a $50 budget, came back with two questions: how you want to interact (talk to it, a touch screen, or a light and button) and whether it should sense the room (camera, air quality or none). Its three picks were all within budget:

  • Waveshare ESP32-C6-Touch-AMOLED-1.8 ($28.99 to $29.99): the cheapest touch screen, but it has no PSRAM, so it can't run the home-network tunnel.
  • AIPI Lite ($35.99): palm-size, with a battery and a two-button menu.
  • Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C ($39.99 to $41.99): the round desk display, with touch and the home-network tunnel.

Answer the questions, choose one, and the agent calls get_build_plan for it. You get the parts, the commands and a brief it can follow step by step. You can compare the same boards yourself on the Muse board comparison.

Who buys the parts: you do

Every shopping list carries the same purchase policy, and the agent is told to follow it:

  • Show you one list with links and the total.
  • Get your explicit approval for the exact items, sellers and total before buying anything.
  • For Amazon and eBay, which don't allow automated carts or checkout, give you the links so you check out yourself.
  • On other stores, add items to a cart and check out only after you approve and ask, with a payment method you already set up.
  • Never type card numbers or passwords.

Hackshop itself never buys anything. If you'd rather shop by hand, the store page lists every board and part with seller and Amazon links.

What your agent can do after planning, and what it can't

With the build plan in hand, a coding agent can do most of the work. Meta's repo has AGENTS.md files written for coding agents. In Meta's words, "Any agent that reads AGENTS.md can build and flash from this repository." Meta's Muse Code runs with --disable-sandbox so it can reach your board's USB serial port. The hackshop brief tells the agent to use ESP-IDF v6.0.1 only, to find the right serial port before flashing, and to keep your SDK token as a placeholder instead of committing it.

Some steps stay with you: approving and paying for parts, pairing the gadget in the Muse app on your phone, and deciding where it lives. The usual Muse terms apply too. SDK tokens are for personal, non-commercial use on up to 50 devices, and Meta says the SDK "may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time." bodyHtml:
AI agent hardware parts come down to a short list: a board that connects to Wi-Fi, usually a screen, a mic and speaker, sometimes a camera or battery, a USB-C cable that carries data, a power supply and something to hold it all. This guide explains each part in plain language, with the specs and prices that matter for a Muse gadget. For the boards covered here, everything plugs together, with no soldering.

Quick answer

Most Muse gadgets with a screen and voice use an ESP32-S3 board with 8 MB of PSRAM, a small LCD or AMOLED screen, a mic and speaker, and a USB-C data cable. Pick a Raspberry Pi instead when you want the agent to run commands on a Linux computer. Pick e-paper for wall displays that change slowly. And check your cable: a charge-only cable can't flash a board.

Microcontroller or single-board computer?

A microcontroller, like Espressif's ESP32 family, is a single chip with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in. It runs one program, the firmware you flash onto it, and needs little power: Espressif puts it at "up to 70mA continuous, 200-300mA peak." In a Muse gadget it handles the screen, buttons, mic and speaker while Muse does the thinking.

A single-board computer, like a Raspberry Pi, runs a full Linux system, usually from a microSD card. Muse's Linux SDK gives the agent a shell, file reads and writes, and a health check. The Pi 5 needs a 5 V, 5 A USB-C supply. Choose a Pi when you want Muse to do sysadmin chores or manage Home Assistant, and remember Meta's warning: "If it can use sudo, so can Muse."

Rule of thumb: for a screen, a talk button and a speaker, pick an ESP32. For a computer the agent can work on, pick a Pi.

AI agent hardware parts compared: the boards

Chip or boardProcessorWirelessRole in a Muse gadgetExample price
ESP32-S3Dual-core Xtensa LX7, 240 MHz2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5 (LE)Most full-UI gadgets: avatar, push-to-talk, imagesStickS3 $21.50; Waveshare 1.75C $39.99 to $41.99
ESP32-C6Single-core RISC-V, up to 160 MHz2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5 (LE), 802.15.4Cheaper touch screens, but no PSRAM on the Waveshare 1.8Waveshare C6 1.8 $28.99 to $29.99
ESP32-C5Single-core RISC-V, up to 240 MHzDual-band Wi-Fi 6 (2.4 and 5 GHz), Bluetooth 5 (LE), 802.15.4Meta's suggested first board: a status light and a buttonDevKitC-1 launched at $15 in 2025
Raspberry Pi Zero 2 WQuad-core Cortex-A53, 1 GHz, 512 MB RAM2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 4.2/BLELight Linux helper: shell and files$15
Raspberry Pi 5Quad-core Cortex-A76, 2.4 GHzDual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0/BLEFull Linux helper$45 (1GB) to $305 (16GB)

Two specs decide what an ESP32 gadget can do. PSRAM is extra working memory. Boards without it, such as the classic ESP32 and the ESP32-C6, can't run Muse's home-network tunnel, though Muse can still reach and control them. Flash stores the firmware: most full-UI builds need 16 MB or more, while the StickS3 and StickC Plus2 use an 8 MB layout. Compare every board's features on the Muse board comparison, or check one you already own with does my board run Muse.

Screens: LCD, AMOLED and e-paper

  • LCD lights its pixels with a backlight. It's cheap and common. Examples: the StickS3's 1.14-inch 135 x 240 screen, the AIPI Lite's 128 x 128, and the SenseCAP Watcher's 1.45-inch 412 x 412 round touch screen.
  • AMOLED pixels make their own light, so black areas are simply off. That gives deep contrast, which suits an avatar face. The Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C has a 1.75-inch 466 x 466 round panel; the Waveshare C6 board has a 1.8-inch 368 x 448 panel.
  • E-paper holds its image between updates. In E Ink's words, "only the regions of the screen that are changing require updating." The Seeed reTerminal E1001 ($69 on sale) has a 7.5-inch 800 x 480 black-and-white panel that refreshes in "a second or two." The color E1002 ($99 on sale) takes about 30 seconds and flashes. Seeed claims "3-month battery life" for both.

Touch matters if you want to tap through settings. The Waveshare boards and the Watcher have touch screens; the StickS3 and AIPI Lite use buttons.

Mics, speakers and cameras

Voice on a Muse gadget is push-to-talk: hold a button, speak, and the board sends a voice note. The Waveshare 1.75C has a dual-mic array. The Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition ($69) pairs its dual mics with a dedicated XMOS XU316 audio processor, and Meta's notes say never to reflash that XMOS chip.

For sound out, the StickS3 has a 1 W speaker and an ES8311 codec. On battery alone, M5Stack recommends keeping its volume below 75% "to avoid unexpected device reboot." The older StickC Plus2 has only a buzzer. Keep in mind that Muse replies in text by default; spoken replies need a text-to-speech service you connect yourself.

For a camera, the Seeed SenseCAP Watcher ($60.99) is the supported pick. Seeed pairs its camera with a "Himax WiseEye2 HX6538 AI chip," and Muse can ask it for a JPEG. Treat it as a privacy decision as much as a parts decision.

Batteries, USB-C data cables and power adapters

Batteries. The StickS3 has a 250 mAh cell built in, and the AIPI Lite comes with a 450 mAh battery module. The Waveshare boards take an optional 3.7 V lithium cell.

Data cables. This is the part that trips up first builds. Meta's SDK requires "A USB cable that carries data, not just power," and Arduino's help center puts it plainly: "Connect your board with a data USB cable, not a charging-only cable." If a board never appears on your computer, try a different cable before anything else. The ESP32 port finder helps once it shows up.

Power adapters. Match the board's rating. The Home Assistant Voice PE takes 5 V at 2 A over USB-C, and the Raspberry Pi 5 wants 5 V at 5 A. The AIPI Lite ships without a USB-C cable or power adapter, so budget for both. Don't run an ESP32 from the 3.3 V output of an FTDI adapter or Arduino board; Espressif says those do "not supply sufficient current." Every part is listed on the store page.

Enclosures and 3D-printed stands

Many supported boards arrive finished. The Waveshare 1.75C comes in a CNC aluminum case, and the AIPI Lite, SenseCAP Watcher, reTerminal panels and Voice PE are complete devices. A stick or bare board needs something to stand in.

Hackshop publishes printable desk stands, as STL and STEP files, for the StickS3, the StickC Plus2 and both Waveshare AMOLED boards. They're small: the StickS3 stand takes about 16 grams of PLA and the round Waveshare stand about 25 grams. At Bambu Lab's $15.99 refill price per kilogram, that's roughly 26 to 39 cents of plastic. PLA is also the easy choice indoors; UL's research says it "generally emits fewer contaminants" than ABS or nylon.

No printer? Some public libraries print for 10 to 20 cents per gram, and online services quote from an uploaded file. Estimate yours with the 3D print cost calculator.

Want to see these parts in place? Take any supported board apart in 3D and tap each part to read what it does.

For the full feature set, yes. Boards without PSRAM, such as the classic ESP32 and the ESP32-C6, can't run Muse's home-network tunnel, though Muse can still reach and control them.

Only if Meta's firmware supports it. The SDK's board table lists 24 ESP32 boards. Others need porting work, so check yours before you buy anything else.

Test it with another device, as Arduino suggests. If the device shows up on your computer, the cable carries data. If it only charges, use a different cable.

Which screen is best for a wall display?

E-paper. It holds its image between updates and suits status or a calendar. The black-and-white reTerminal E1001 refreshes in a second or two; the color E1002 takes about 30 seconds and flashes.

It does a different job. A Pi gives Muse a Linux computer to run commands on, with no screen or speaker. An ESP32 board gives Muse a face, a button and a speaker on far less power.

title: Push-to-Talk vs Always Listening for AI Devices

Should Your AI Gadget Always Listen?
job: Choose between push-to-talk, a wake word and always-on listening for an AI gadget, and know which Muse boards support which.
tweet: Push-to-talk, wake word or always listening? For a DIY AI gadget, push-to-talk wins on privacy, false triggers and battery, and every voice board in Meta's Muse SDK uses it today. Here is how the modes compare.
video: Side by side on a desk: a TV plays next to a wake-word speaker and a push-to-talk StickS3, showing which one wakes up on its own.
description: Push-to-talk vs always listening for an AI gadget: how each mode and wake words handle privacy, false triggers and battery, and which Muse boards do which.

sources.label: Muse ESP32 SDK AGENTS.md (Voice PE notes)
Muse ESP32 SDK supported devices and features
Mon(IoT)r Research Group: When Speakers Are All Ears

faq.q: Do Muse gadgets support a wake word?
faq.a: Not according to the SDK documentation. Every board in the Muse ESP32 SDK that has a microphone is listed with push-to-talk, and none is listed with a wake word. The code is open source under Apache 2.0, so you could add one, but you would be building and tuning it yourself.

faq.q: Is push-to-talk more private than a wake word?
faq.a: In most homes, yes. Push-to-talk records only while someone holds the button, so the TV or a conversation can't set it off. A wake-word device can also be private, but every misfire starts a recording of whatever is said next.

faq.q: Will my gadget answer out loud?
faq.a: Not by default. Muse replies with text, which boards with screens show as captions and the Voice PE shows in the Muse app. For spoken answers, you send each reply to a text-to-speech API of your choice and play the audio it returns.

faq.q: Does the Voice PE mute switch still work with Muse firmware?
faq.a: Home Assistant says the switch physically cuts power to the microphones, which is a hardware action rather than a software setting. In the Muse build, turning it on also returns the center button to its setup role for pairing and resets.

bodyHtml:
Push-to-talk vs always listening is really a question about who opens the microphone. With push-to-talk, you do, by holding a button. With a wake word, a small detector on the device listens for a phrase and opens it for you. An always-listening device processes sound all the time. If you are building an AI gadget with Meta's Muse Gadgets SDK today, the choice is simple: every voice board in the SDK uses push-to-talk.

Quick answer

Push-to-talk is the most private and battery-friendly mode and almost never fires by accident, but you need a free hand. A wake word is hands-free but can trigger by mistake. Always listening costs the most in battery and privacy. On Muse gadgets, the SDK lists push-to-talk for every board with a microphone and documents no wake-word mode.

The three listening modes in plain terms

All three modes can run on the same hardware: a microphone, a chip and a network connection. What changes is the rule for when sound gets recorded and sent anywhere.

  • Push-to-talk. The mic records only while you hold a button. On a Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition running the Muse firmware, holding the center button records a voice note that Muse answers in the Muse app.
  • Wake word. The device runs a small detector nonstop and starts recording after it hears a set phrase. Home Assistant's own firmware for the same Voice PE does this on the device with an engine called microWakeWord, listening for "Okay Nabu", "Hey Jarvis" or "Hey Mycroft".
  • Always listening. The device processes all the audio it hears, for example to transcribe a meeting or react to sounds. None of the Muse gadget builds work this way.

So the same $69 Voice PE can be a wake-word speaker for Home Assistant or a push-to-talk speaker for Muse. It depends on the firmware you flash.

The tradeoff is convenience. Push-to-talk wins on almost everything except the moment your hands are covered in flour.

Privacy: who controls the microphone

Push-to-talk gives you the simplest rule to explain to everyone in the house: nothing is recorded unless someone is holding the button. On Muse gadgets, that voice note goes to Muse, which transcribes it and answers in writing. Muse's homepage says your conversations "are not shared with Meta's ad systems".

A wake-word device has a harder job. Its detector has to hear everything to find the phrase. On the Voice PE's stock firmware, Home Assistant says that detection runs on the device. The weak spot is the mistakes: every false trigger starts a recording of whatever is said next.

Hardware switches help with either mode. Home Assistant says the Voice PE's mute switch "physically cuts power to the microphones". In the Muse build, turning the switch on also gives the center button back its setup role, so you can confirm pairing or hold it for 5 seconds to reset.

False triggers: how often wake words misfire

Wake words misfire because TV, music and conversation are full of sounds that resemble the phrase. Researchers from Northeastern University and Imperial College London tested this by playing 125 hours of Netflix shows to smart speakers including the Echo Dot, Google Home Mini, HomePod and Harman Kardon Invoke. They measured an average of 1.5 to 19 accidental activations per device per day, depending on the device, and the longest ones lasted 20 to 43 seconds.

Push-to-talk avoids this almost entirely. Its version of a false trigger is an accidental press, such as a pocket device bumping against your keys. That is easier to notice and easier to prevent, for example by carrying the device in a case.

If you add your own wake word to a gadget later, plan for misfires from day one: give people a visible sign that the mic is open and a simple way to mute it.

Battery: why push-to-talk lasts longer

A wake word needs the microphone and some processing running every second the device is on. Push-to-talk lets the board wait for a button. That matters most on pocket boards, which have small batteries: the M5Stack StickS3 has a 250 mAh cell, and the AIPI Lite comes with a 450 mAh battery module.

The Muse firmware helps here too. When you power the StickS3 off from Muse, it turns off the screen, speaker and audio codec and puts the ESP32-S3 into deep sleep, and either button wakes it. M5Stack also advises keeping the speaker volume below 75% on battery alone "to avoid unexpected device reboot".

Plugged-in boards care less. The Voice PE runs from USB-C at 5 V and 2 A, so for that board the choice is purely about privacy and convenience.

How to choose a listening mode for your build

  • Shared rooms and kitchens: push-to-talk with a hardware mute is the easiest setup to trust. The Voice PE gives you both.
  • On the go: a pocket board with a front button works like a walkie-talkie for your agent. The StickS3 is a low-cost full-UI option at $21.50.
  • At your desk: pick a board with a screen so you can read replies, such as the Waveshare 1.75C or the Watcher. The desk companion comparison covers the three main picks.
  • You truly need hands-free: be honest about the work. A wake word is not in the Muse SDK today, so you would be adding and tuning it yourself.

Questions people ask

Do Muse gadgets support a wake word?

Not according to the SDK documentation. Every board in the Muse ESP32 SDK that has a microphone is listed with push-to-talk, and none is listed with a wake word. The code is open source under Apache 2.0, so you could add one, but you would be building and tuning it yourself.

Is push-to-talk more private than a wake word?

In most homes, yes. Push-to-talk records only while someone holds the button, so the TV or a conversation can't set it off. A wake-word device can also be private, but every misfire starts a recording of whatever is said next.

Will my gadget answer out loud?

Not by default. Muse replies with text, which boards with screens show as captions and the Voice PE shows in the Muse app. For spoken answers, you send each reply to a text-to-speech API of your choice and play the audio it returns.

Does the Voice PE mute switch still work with Muse firmware?

Home Assistant says the switch physically cuts power to the microphones, which is a hardware action rather than a software setting. In the Muse build, turning it on also returns the center button to its setup role for pairing and resets.

bodyHtml:
Where should your AI agent live? Put its body where you will actually use it: on your desk if you want to read replies and talk to it, in your pocket if you want a voice remote, on a wall or fridge if the household needs to glance at it, and out of sight if it does background work. Each spot changes which board fits, how you power it and how much the Wi-Fi signal matters.

Quick answer

For a desk, pick a screen with push-to-talk, like the Waveshare round AMOLED or the SenseCAP Watcher. For a pocket, pick the M5Stack StickS3 or the AIPI Lite. For a wall or fridge, pick a reTerminal e-paper display. For a hidden helper, pick a Raspberry Pi or the ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1. Check the outlet and the Wi-Fi signal at the spot before you buy.

Where should your AI agent live? The four spots compared

SpotGood forBoards that fitPowerNetwork notes
DeskReading replies, an avatar, quick voice notesWaveshare S3 1.75C, SenseCAP Watcher, AIPI Lite, Waveshare C6 1.8, ideaspark 1.9", Voice PE, SenseCAP Indicator, reTerminalUSB from a charger; some boards have batteriesUsually close to the router
PocketVoice notes away from your deskM5Stack StickS3, AIPI Lite, M5Stack StickC Plus2Small built-in batteryNeeds a Wi-Fi network it already knows
Wall or fridgeGlanceable info for everyone at homereTerminal E1001 and E1002, SenseCAP IndicatorBattery on the reTerminals; USB for the IndicatorTest the signal at the exact spot
HiddenBackground jobs and reaching your home networkRaspberry Pi 5, 4 or Zero 2 W, ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1, Voice PE, used thin clientsWall powerEthernet on a Pi 5; Linux pairing needs Bluetooth LE

These fits come from hackshop's board data, and a few boards fit two spots.

Desk: see it and talk to it

A desk is the easiest first home. Power is close, the router is usually in range, and you can read what your agent says. Pick a board with a screen and push-to-talk.

  • Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C: a round 1.75" 466×466 AMOLED touch screen with an animated avatar. hackshop rates it the best desk object. It lists at $39.99 to $41.99, and the higher price appears to be the version with a battery.
  • Seeed SenseCAP Watcher: a 1.45" round touch screen, a wheel you press to talk, and a camera Muse can use once you enable it in the build. It costs $60.99.
  • AIPI Lite: a palm-size voice buddy at $35.99 with a 128×128 screen and a snap-on battery.
  • Budget picks: the Waveshare ESP32-C6-Touch-AMOLED-1.8 does push-to-talk with text replies, and the ideaspark 1.9" board is a small status screen that can show pictures.

Angle the screen toward where you sit. Replies arrive as text captions, and a small screen is easier to read up close.

Pocket: a push-to-talk remote

A pocket body turns your agent into a walkie-talkie. You press a button, say what you need, and read the reply when it arrives.

  • M5Stack StickS3: $21.50, 48×24×15 mm and 20 g, with a speaker, a mic, a 1.14" screen and a 250 mAh battery. hackshop calls it the best push-to-talk remote. M5Stack recommends keeping the speaker below 75% volume on battery to avoid reboots.
  • AIPI Lite: comes with a 450 mAh battery module but no USB-C cable or power adapter, so have a cable ready.
  • M5Stack StickC Plus2: still supported by the SDK, but listed as end of life, and it has a buzzer instead of a speaker.

The catch is Wi-Fi. A pocket board still needs a network it knows, and ESP32-S3 boards use 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only. The documented way to move a board to a new network is to reset setup, which unpairs it and forgets its Wi-Fi, and then pair it again in the Muse app. In practice, it is an around-the-house device.

Wall or fridge: glanceable and quiet

A wall or fridge body is for things the whole household reads in passing. Meta's gadget page suggests a morning briefing, reminders or a shopping list on the color e-paper reTerminal. These boards show status and images but have no microphone in the Muse build, so you talk to your agent from your phone and the display shows the result.

  • Seeed reTerminal E1002: 7.3" six-color e-paper, $99 on sale (regular $109). Each refresh takes about 30 seconds and flashes, so it suits content that changes a few times a day.
  • Seeed reTerminal E1001: 7.5" black-and-white e-paper, $69 on sale (regular $79). A refresh takes a second or two.
  • Seeed SenseCAP Indicator: a 3.95" touch screen that fits a desk or a wall. The D1S and D1Pro models add air sensors. It has no battery, so it needs an outlet nearby.

E-paper keeps its picture without power, and Seeed advertises a "3-month battery life" for both reTerminals. Treat that as the maker's figure and watch how your own build behaves. If you plan to put one on a fridge, test the Wi-Fi there first, since a fridge door is a big sheet of metal. For a full wall build, see the guide to a family calendar on e-paper.

Hidden: background work and home-network reach

Some agent bodies don't need a face. A hidden gadget sits in a closet or behind the TV and gives Muse a way to work on a computer or reach devices on your home network.

  • Raspberry Pi 5 with the Linux Device SDK: Muse can run shell commands, read and write files and check the machine's health. List prices are $110 for 4GB and $175 for 8GB. It has Gigabit Ethernet, dual-band Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE for pairing, and it needs a 5 V, 5 A USB-C power supply.
  • Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W: $15, with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only. It is slow, but enough for shell and file commands.
  • ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1: the SDK's suggested quickest start, with a status light, a button and the home-network tunnel, which lets Muse reach devices you own that have a local HTTP API. Its chip supports dual-band Wi-Fi 6.
  • Used thin clients such as the Dell Wyse 5070: not on Meta's list, but they meet the stated requirements on Debian or Ubuntu once they have Bluetooth LE, which usually means a USB adapter.

Hidden does not mean forgotten. Put the board where you can still see its status light now and then: green means connected, blinking yellow means reconnecting and blinking red means an error. Also remember that a Linux gadget gives Muse the same access as the account you install it for. If that account can use sudo, so can Muse.

Power and Wi-Fi checklist before you pick a spot

  • An outlet in reach. Desk and hidden boards run from USB power. The Voice PE takes 5 V at 2 A over USB-C, and a Pi 5 needs a 5 V, 5 A USB-C supply.
  • A data cable for setup. You flash ESP32 boards over USB, and the cable must carry data, not just power.
  • 2.4 GHz coverage. ESP32-S3 boards use 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, and AIPI says the AIPI Lite needs it. The ESP32-C5 and the Pi 5 can also use 5 GHz.
  • Signal at the exact spot. Check it with your phone where the gadget will actually sit.
  • A trusted network for pairing. The SDK warns that pairing can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack, so pair at home.

Not sure which spot fits your routine? The Muse board picker suggests a board from a few questions, and the Muse board guide compares every supported board side by side.

Can one gadget cover more than one spot?

Yes. In hackshop's board data, the AIPI Lite fits a desk or a pocket, the reTerminal e-paper displays and the SenseCAP Indicator fit a desk or a wall, and the Home Assistant Voice PE fits a desk or a hidden shelf.

Will a pocket gadget work away from home?

Only where it has Wi-Fi it knows. ESP32 boards join the network you set up in the Muse app, and the documented way to change networks is to reset setup and pair again. Treat a pocket gadget as an around-the-house device.

What is the best spot for a first build?

A desk. Power and Wi-Fi are close, you can see the status and read replies, and it is easy to plug the board back into your computer when you want to flash it again.

Does a wall e-paper display need to stay plugged in?

No. The reTerminal E1001 and E1002 have batteries, and e-paper keeps its picture without power. Seeed advertises a 3-month battery life, so treat that as the maker's figure and check how your own build does.

An AI agent body today can listen when you press a button, show its status and replies on a light or screen, take a photo, read air sensors and run commands on a computer. It can't move, pick things up or work without Wi-Fi and the cloud. This is an honest list of what a small AI agent body does, based on Meta's Muse Gadgets SDK and the boards hackshop supports.

Quick answer

Think of a small agent body as senses and a face, not a robot. It can hear you through push-to-talk, show you things on lights, screens and e-paper, see with one camera board, sense the air with one sensor board, and act on computers and devices on your network. It has no motors or arms, it needs Wi-Fi and Muse's cloud to think, it replies in text unless you add speech, and pocket batteries are small.

What an AI agent body can do today

The thinking happens in the cloud. Every Muse board pairs with the Muse app, joins your Wi-Fi and holds an encrypted session to Muse. The board is the part that hears, shows and senses.

Listen when you press a button

Boards with a mic use push-to-talk. You hold a button, the board sends a voice note, and Muse transcribes it and answers. The M5Stack StickS3, AIPI Lite, Waveshare round AMOLED, SenseCAP Watcher and Home Assistant Voice PE all work this way. The SDK docs don't describe a wake word.

Show status, text and pictures

Even the simplest board shows what it is doing. The ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1 uses a single status light: breathing orange for setup, green for connected and blinking red for an error. Screen boards show an animated avatar and Muse's replies as captions, and many can display pictures Muse sends. The reTerminal e-paper displays show a still status screen and black-and-white or six-color images.

See with a camera

The SenseCAP Watcher is the camera board. Camera support is off by default. Once you enable it in the build, Muse can call camera.capture and get back a JPEG. A capture takes under a second, start-up included, and the camera is powered only while a capture or the live view runs.

Sense the air

The SenseCAP Indicator D1S and D1Pro have built-in CO2 and tVOC sensors, and temperature and humidity come from a Grove AHT20 sensor included in the box. Muse reads them all at once with sensors.read. This needs Seeed's stock RP2040 firmware left in place.

Act on computers and your network

On a Raspberry Pi or another Linux box, Muse can run shell commands, read and write files, and check uptime, load, memory, disk and temperature. Programs on that machine can message Muse too. On ESP32 boards with PSRAM, the home-network tunnel lets Muse reach devices you own that have a local HTTP API. You can also add your own commands, such as reading a sensor or switching a relay.

Can and cannot, at a glance

AbilityWhat works todayLimits

Answer youText captions, or the Muse app on the Voice PESpoken replies need your own text-to-speech API
Show thingsStatus lights, an LED ring, screens and e-paperThe color E1002 takes about 30 seconds per refresh
SeeWatcher camera, when Muse asks for a photoNo photo attachments on voice notes
SenseAir sensors on the Indicator D1S and D1ProExtras like the StickS3's motion sensor aren't used yet
ActLinux commands, local HTTP devices, your own commandsCannot move, roll, grab or lift
Work offlineNoNeeds Wi-Fi and Muse's cloud

What it cannot do yet

Move

None of the boards hackshop supports has wheels, motors or arms. They stay where you put them. You can wire a relay and add a command so Muse can switch something on or off, but that is a switch, not a robot. hackshop doesn't plan robot kits that move yet, so a rolling or walking agent is a fully custom project for now.

Work without Wi-Fi and the cloud

No network, no agent. ESP32-S3 boards need 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, and the brain lives in Muse's cloud. Meta's terms also say the SDK and tokens "are not a supported product" and "may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time". Cloud devices do get switched off: Humane's AI Pin stopped answering queries when its service shut down on February 28, 2025. The difference here is that the firmware is open source and builds never turn on Secure Boot, so you can reflash the board for something else.

Answer instantly

Every reply makes a round trip to the cloud, and some parts are slow by design. The E1002 refresh takes about 30 seconds, custom commands time out after 30 seconds by default unless you raise the limit, and redrawing your avatar takes several minutes, mostly waiting for Muse. The SDK docs give no reply-time figures for voice, so test on your own network before you rely on it for anything urgent.

Speak out loud by default

Muse replies in text. For spoken answers, you hook a text-to-speech API into the firmware. The StickC Plus2 has only a buzzer, and the Voice PE shows replies in the Muse app.

Run for days on a small battery

Pocket boards have small cells: 250 mAh in the StickS3 and a 450 mAh module with the AIPI Lite. M5Stack advises keeping the StickS3 below 75% volume on battery to avoid reboots. E-paper is the exception, with Seeed advertising a 3-month battery life for its reTerminal displays.

Match the body to the job

  • A face to talk to: a round screen like the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C.
  • Eyes on your desk: the SenseCAP Watcher with its camera turned on.
  • Air you can ask about: the SenseCAP Indicator, in the D1S or D1Pro version.
  • Hands on a computer: a Raspberry Pi with the Linux SDK. The guide to Muse on a Raspberry Pi covers the setup.
  • A voice remote: the StickS3, at $21.50.

Not with the boards hackshop supports today. None has wheels, motors or arms, and hackshop doesn't plan robot kits that move yet. You can add a relay command so Muse switches something on or off, which is useful but is not a robot.

faq.a: It is a reasonable choice for gadgets that only need to reach Muse, like a desk companion or an e-paper display. If you want Muse to reach other devices through the gadget's home-network tunnel, those devices need to be reachable from the network the gadget is on.

bodyHtml:
AI gadget home network security is mostly ordinary hygiene done on purpose. Pair the gadget on a network you trust, keep your router and firmware current, give the device only the access it needs, and know what it sends to the cloud. A DIY Muse gadget is a small computer with a microphone, sometimes a camera, and a link to your agent, so it deserves the same care as any other connected device in your home.

Quick answer

Use WPA3 or WPA2 on your router and change its default passwords. Pair the gadget at home. Keep your SDK token out of git and turn on NVS encryption. On a Raspberry Pi, run the gadget under an account without sudo unless you need it. Point any camera at a desk, not a bedroom. Back up a board's original flash before you install Muse, and only flash firmware you built from the official repo.

What data leaves an AI gadget

Start by knowing what actually crosses the network. This table comes from Meta's SDK docs. For anything beyond it, read Muse's privacy policy rather than guessing.

PartWhat leaves the deviceWhen
ConnectionPairing with your phone over Bluetooth LE, then an encrypted session to Muse over Wi-FiAt setup, then while it is on
MicrophoneYour voice note, which Muse transcribesOnly while you hold push-to-talk
Camera (Watcher)A JPEGWhen Muse requests a capture; off by default in the build
Air sensors (Indicator)CO2, tVOC, temperature and humidity readingsWhen Muse reads them
Home-network tunnelTraffic between Muse and your devices with a local HTTP APIWhen Muse uses those devices
Linux gadgetCommand output and file contentsWhen Muse runs a command or reads a file

On the agent side, Muse's homepage says you approve actions such as sending emails and making purchases before they happen, and that your conversations "are not shared with Meta's ad systems".

AI gadget home network security starts at the router

The FTC's home Wi-Fi advice covers most of what you need:

  • Use WPA3 Personal or WPA2 Personal encryption.
  • Change the router's default admin username, password and network name.
  • Keep the router's software up to date.
  • Turn off remote management, WPS and UPnP.
  • Turn on the router's firewall.

Then pair the gadget at home, not on a coffee shop network. Meta's SDK says pairing "has no manufacturer verification and can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack. Set it up on a network you trust." Pairing does require a press of the button on the device, and every setup creates a fresh encrypted session.

Should it go on a guest or IoT network?

The FTC suggests setting up a guest network with its own name and password. A separate network is a good fit for gadgets that only talk to Muse, like a desk companion or an e-paper display. The tradeoff is reach: a gadget can only get to what its own network can. If you want the home-network tunnel to reach your smart plugs or a local HTTP service, those devices need to be reachable from the gadget's network. Also make sure that network offers 2.4 GHz, since ESP32-S3 boards use 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.

Lock down the gadget itself

  • Treat the SDK token as an identifier, not a password. It ships inside the firmware. Still, never commit it to git or paste it in full anywhere. If it leaks, revoke it on gadgets.muse.ai, generate a new one and rebuild.
  • Turn on NVS encryption. The board stores Wi-Fi credentials and device tokens in flash, and without encryption anyone with physical access can read them. The README strongly recommends enabling CONFIG_HOMEHUB_NVS_ENCRYPTION if your board supports it.
  • Leave Secure Boot off. The SDK says never to enable Secure Boot, flash encryption or eFuse pairing auth on a board you want to keep reflashing.
  • Mind where the board sits. Anyone with physical access can read an unencrypted board, so keep it somewhere strangers can't quietly pick it up or plug into it.
  • On a Raspberry Pi, limit the account. Muse gets the same access as the account you install it for: "If it can use sudo, so can Muse." The README tells you to read install.sh before you run it, and --run-as lets you give Muse an account without sudo.

The guide to Muse on a Raspberry Pi covers the Linux setup step by step.

Updates without surprises

Boards with the full on-screen UI, such as the StickS3 and the Waveshare round AMOLED, have over-the-air updates turned on. Other boards, including the ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1, the reTerminals and the Voice PE, have them off by default, so you update them by pulling the latest code and reflashing. Reflashing keeps your pairing and Wi-Fi settings, while erase-flash wipes them.

Keep the router updated too. And remember that Meta's terms say the SDK "may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time", so check the repo now and then.

Microphone and camera habits

  • Push-to-talk by design. Voice boards record only while someone holds the button. The trade-offs are covered in push-to-talk vs always listening.
  • Use the hardware mute. Home Assistant says the Voice PE mute switch "physically cuts power to the microphones".
  • Place cameras with care. The SenseCAP Watcher camera is off by default. If you turn it on, aim it at a desk, shelf or doorway, not a bedroom or bathroom, and tell the people you live with. It is powered only while a capture or the live view runs.
  • Be upfront when you give one away. Meta's terms say you must tell the other person, before they pair it, what the device does with their information, and you may not keep or reuse their prompts or data.

Don't flash random firmware, and back up first

Only flash firmware you built from the official facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk repo, or code you have read. If a coding agent does the work, Muse Code still asks you to approve each command before it runs. Meta's own page is plain about the risk: "Side effects of tinkering may include bricked boards, voided warranties, brownouts, or bankruptcies."

Before the first Muse flash, save the board's original data:

  • SenseCAP Watcher: Muse overwrites its factory data, which is unique to each Watcher. Back up the nvsfactory partition with the SDK's paced tool: tools/muse/paced_esptool.py --chip esp32s3 -p PORT read-flash 0x9000 0x32000 nvsfactory.bin. Plain esptool fails on the Watcher's USB bridge.
  • M5Stack StickS3: back up the full 8 MB flash with read-flash 0 0x800000 sticks3.bin so you can return to UiFlow2.
  • M5Stack StickC Plus2: back up the flash at 230400 baud before the first flash.
  • Home Assistant Voice PE: Muse replaces the firmware on the ESP32-S3 only. Never reflash the XMOS audio chip.

Keep backups out of git and somewhere you will find them later.

Questions people ask

Should I put my AI gadget on a guest network?

It is a reasonable choice for gadgets that only need to reach Muse, like a desk companion or an e-paper display. If you want Muse to reach other devices through the gadget's home-network tunnel, those devices need to be reachable from the network the gadget is on.

Is the Muse SDK token a password?

No. Meta says to treat it as an identifier, because it ships inside the firmware. Keep it out of git anyway, and if it leaks, revoke it on gadgets.muse.ai, create a new one and rebuild.

Does a Muse gadget listen all the time?

The voice boards in the SDK use push-to-talk, so they record a voice note only while you hold the button. The SDK docs don't describe a wake word.

What should I do if I lose a gadget?

Revoke your SDK token on gadgets.muse.ai and rebuild your other gadgets with a new one. If NVS encryption was off, also change your Wi-Fi password, since the board stored it in flash.

Looking for AI agent body ideas that actually work? Here are 15 builds you can make today with off-the-shelf boards and Meta's Muse Gadgets SDK, from a round desk companion to a family calendar on e-paper. Each one uses a board hackshop supports and only asks the board to do what its docs say it can.

Quick answer

The easiest starts are a desk companion on the Waveshare round AMOLED, a pocket voice note taker on the $21.50 M5Stack StickS3, and a morning briefing on a reTerminal e-paper display. If you have a spare Raspberry Pi, turn it into a home server helper. Every idea below links to its board page.

Desk AI agent body ideas

1. Round desk companion

A 1.75" round AMOLED touch screen with an animated avatar, push-to-talk and replies as captions. You can even ask Muse to redraw its avatar for the screen. Board: Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C, $39.99 to $41.99.

2. Desk camera helper

Ask Muse to look at your whiteboard or the parts on your bench. Once you enable the camera in the build, Muse can take a photo and get a JPEG back. Board: Seeed SenseCAP Watcher, $60.99.

3. Air-quality monitor

From the Muse app, ask whether the room is stuffy, and Muse reads CO2, tVOC, temperature and humidity in one call. Only the D1S and D1Pro have the air sensors, and temperature and humidity come from the Grove sensor in the box. Board: Seeed SenseCAP Indicator.

4. Glanceable status screen

A small color screen that shows what Muse is up to and any picture it sends. It has no PSRAM, so it skips the home-network tunnel. Board: ideaspark ESP32 with 1.9" LCD.

5. Budget text-reply buddy

Push-to-talk on a 1.8" AMOLED touch screen, with replies scrolling past as text. Without PSRAM it can't show images or run the tunnel, but it is a low-cost way to try a talking gadget. Board: Waveshare ESP32-C6-Touch-AMOLED-1.8.

Pocket and kitchen ideas

6. Pocket voice note taker

Press the front button, say the thought, and Muse transcribes it and answers in text on the 1.14" screen. It weighs 20 g and has a 250 mAh battery. Board: M5Stack StickS3, $21.50.

7. Kitchen recipe helper

Keep a palm-size buddy on the counter for quick questions like unit conversions, and let Muse show a picture on its color screen. It is push-to-talk, so press with a clean knuckle. Timers aren't a documented feature, so keep your oven timer for that. Board: AIPI Lite, $35.99.

8. Shelf voice point

A speaker-mic puck for the living room. Hold the center button to talk, watch status on the LED ring, set volume with the dial and read replies in the Muse app. Its mute switch cuts power to the mics. Board: Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition, $69.

Wall and fridge ideas

9. Family calendar and morning briefing

A 7.3" six-color e-paper display where Muse posts the day's plan, reminders or a morning briefing. Each refresh takes about 30 seconds and flashes, so update it a few times a day, not every minute. Board: Seeed reTerminal E1002, $99 on sale.

10. Shopping list by the fridge

Black-and-white e-paper refreshes in a second or two, which suits a list that changes as people add items from their phones. It keeps its picture without power. Board: Seeed reTerminal E1001, $69 on sale.

Out-of-sight helpers

11. Home server helper

Install the Linux Device SDK and ask things like "What's using all the disk space on my Pi?", or have Muse check each morning whether your backups ran. It can even install Home Assistant for you. Board: Raspberry Pi 5, $110 for 4GB at list price.

12. Sensor alert relay

Any program on the Pi can message Muse with musegadget send-user-msg, such as "The garage door has been open for an hour." You supply the sensor and the script. Board: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, $15.

13. Smart ring note bridge

The Linux SDK includes an example webhook listener that sends every note from a Pebble ring to its own Muse chat. Any supported Pi can run it. Board: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.

14. Second life for a thin client

A used office thin client can be an always-on Linux box for Muse. It isn't on Meta's list, but it meets the stated requirements on Debian or Ubuntu once it has Bluetooth LE, usually from a USB adapter. Board: Dell Wyse 5070.

15. Busy light by your door

Out of the box, the status light shows connection state. Ask your coding agent to add a command that sets the light's color, and Muse can turn it red when you are on a call. This one needs a small code change. Board: Espressif ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1.

bodyHtml:
The best Muse gadget setups start with one question: what should your agent do in the room? For most people the answer is a desk companion with a screen and push-to-talk, and the best device for Meta Muse in that role is the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C at $39.99. Other goals call for other boards. Below are six setups, each with a board, a price, pros, cons and who it suits.

Quick answer

Desk companion: Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C ($39.99, or $41.99 with a battery). Pocket voice: M5Stack StickS3 ($21.50). Wall or fridge display: Seeed reTerminal E1002 ($99 on sale). E-paper calendar: Seeed reTerminal E1001 ($69 on sale). Camera: Seeed SenseCAP Watcher ($60.99). Linux box: Raspberry Pi 5 4GB ($110 list) or Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W ($15). Prices checked October 5, 2026.

How to pick a Muse gadget setup

Muse Gadgets is Meta's open source project for turning off-the-shelf ESP32 boards and Raspberry Pi or Linux boxes into devices for Muse, Meta's personal AI agent. The ESP32 SDK lists 24 boards, and every option falls into one of three tiers:

  • Status boards show what Muse is doing on a light, an LED ring, a small screen or e-paper. Several also show images Muse sends.
  • Full UI boards run an animated avatar, push-to-talk and on-screen settings. Most also show images.
  • Linux boxes run Meta's Linux Device SDK, which lets Muse run shell commands, read and write files, and check the machine's health.

Pick by goal first, then by budget. Every gadget needs an SDK token from gadgets.muse.ai and pairs with the Muse app on iOS or Android with Developer mode on. For a guided pick, the Muse board picker quiz asks a few questions and suggests a board, and the Muse board guide lists every supported board side by side.

Best Muse gadget setups compared

The six setups in detail

1. Desk companion with a screen and voice: Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C

This round board is one of Meta's featured example projects, and it looks like a finished object on a desk. It has a 1.75-inch 466×466 AMOLED touch screen, a dual-mic array, a speaker and a CNC aluminum case. Waveshare sells it for $39.99 without a battery or $41.99 with a 3.7 V lithium battery that fits inside the case.

  • Pros: a round AMOLED screen with touch settings, push-to-talk, over-the-air updates, and enough memory for images and the home-network tunnel.
  • Cons: no camera, and a small screen for reading long replies.
  • Who it's for: anyone who wants one Muse gadget that lives on the desk and looks good doing it.

A cheaper alternative is the AIPI Lite ($35.99), a palm-size buddy with a 128×128 screen and a 450 mAh battery module. Parts and stands for the Waveshare are on its board page.

2. Pocket voice remote: M5Stack StickS3

The StickS3 is a 48×24×15 mm stick that weighs 20 g and costs $21.50 from M5Stack. It has a 1.14-inch color screen, a MEMS mic, a 1 W speaker and a 250 mAh battery. The front button is push-to-talk and the side button steps through the menu.

  • Pros: the cheapest full UI board here, fits in a pocket, and runs the avatar UI and images.
  • Cons: a tiny screen, and a fussier first flash, because it ships with UiFlow2, which switches off the chip's USB serial port. On battery alone, M5Stack recommends keeping speaker volume below 75% to avoid unexpected reboots.
  • Who it's for: people who want to talk to Muse from anywhere in the house.

Skip the older StickC Plus2: the SDK lists it as end of life, and it only has a buzzer. See the StickS3 board page for the flashing workaround.

3. Wall or fridge display: Seeed reTerminal E1002

Meta pitches this board as a color e-ink display where Muse "can show a morning briefing, reminders, shopping list, or anything else you think of." It has a 7.3-inch 800×480 E Ink Spectra 6 panel with six colors and a built-in battery. Seeed has it on sale at $99 (regular $109).

  • Pros: large and readable, keeps its picture with no power, runs on battery, and shows color images Muse sends.
  • Cons: each refresh takes about 30 seconds and flashes, so it's for still pictures only. No voice and no touch.
  • Who it's for: households that want a shared board in the kitchen or hallway.

Prefer a bright live screen and have an outlet nearby? The Seeed SenseCAP Indicator D1 ($49) has a 4-inch 480×480 LCD that shows status and color images, but no battery.

4. E-paper calendar: Seeed reTerminal E1001

The E1001 is the same board as the E1002 with a 7.5-inch 800×480 black and white panel. Each refresh takes "a second or two", and it costs $69 on sale (regular $79).

  • Pros: quick refresh, lower price, and crisp black and white text for schedules and lists.
  • Cons: no color, images are dithered to black and white, and there's no voice.
  • Who it's for: families who want a calendar or chore board that changes several times a day.

The Muse family calendar guide covers both reTerminals.

5. Camera: Seeed SenseCAP Watcher

The Watcher is the only board where the Muse SDK supports a camera. Around its ESP32-S3, Seeed adds a Himax WiseEye2 HX6538 AI chip, a camera, a mic and a speaker, plus a 1.45-inch 412×412 round touch screen and a scroll wheel. It costs $60.99.

  • Pros: Muse can call camera.capture and get back a JPEG, and you get a live view on the screen.
  • Cons: the camera is off until you turn on a build option, and photos can't be attached to voice messages. The first flash is the hardest here: you back up its unique factory partition, pick the right one of two USB ports (the one ending in 3), and wait about three minutes while the flash shows nothing.
  • Who it's for: tinkerers who want Muse to see what's on the desk.

The Watcher build steps walk through the backup and the slow flash.

6. Linux box: Raspberry Pi 5 or Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W

The Linux Device SDK turns a Raspberry Pi with Bluetooth (a 3B+, 4, 5 or Zero 2 W) into a Muse gadget with no firmware flashing. Muse gets four built-in commands: run a shell command, read a file, write a file and report the machine's health. Meta suggests it for sysadmin chores or your Home Assistant setup.

  • Pros: one install script, room to run real apps, and programs on the Pi can send messages to Muse with musegadget send-user-msg.
  • Cons: no voice or screen out of the box, and Muse gets the same access as the account you install it for, sudo included. Pi 5 prices also rose twice in 2026: the 4GB now lists at $110 and the 8GB at $175.
  • Who it's for: people who run a home server, or want Muse to set one up. A Zero 2 W at $15 is enough for shell and file jobs.

The Raspberry Pi 5 build steps list the power supply and card you need.

Other boards worth knowing

  • Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition ($69 MSRP): push-to-talk, status on an LED ring and a volume dial. Replies show up in the Muse app, not on the device.
  • Espressif ESP32-C5 DevKitC-1: the SDK's suggested quickest start. It "works as-is with its built-in status light and BOOT button".
  • ideaspark ESP32 with 1.9" display: a small color status screen that shows images. It has no PSRAM, so it can't run the home-network tunnel.
  • Waveshare ESP32-C6-Touch-AMOLED-1.8: a larger touch screen, but no PSRAM, so replies scroll past as text and it can't show images.

Already own an ESP32 board or a spare Pi? Check it with Does my board run Muse? before you buy anything.

What every setup can and can't do

  • Voice is push-to-talk. You press a button and talk, Muse transcribes your voice note and answers in writing.
  • Spoken replies take extra work. You connect a text-to-speech API at the SDK's start_tts hook.
  • Memory matters. Boards without PSRAM can't run the home-network tunnel that lets Muse reach other devices on your Wi-Fi.
  • ESP32 flashing has fixed needs. A USB cable that carries data, a Mac or Linux computer, and ESP-IDF version 6.0.1 exactly. Muse Code, or any coding agent that reads the SDK's AGENTS.md, can do the build and flash.
  • Pairing isn't verified by a manufacturer. The SDK says it "can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack", so set gadgets up on a network you trust.
  • It's a hobby platform. Meta says the SDK and tokens "are not a supported product and not a developer platform" and may change or stop working. Tokens are for personal, non-commercial use.

Questions people ask

What is the best device for Meta Muse?

For most people, the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C ($39.99): a round AMOLED touch screen, push-to-talk, a speaker and two mics. Pick the M5Stack StickS3 ($21.50) for a pocket remote, a Seeed reTerminal for a wall display, the SenseCAP Watcher for a camera, or a Raspberry Pi for a Linux box.

Not out of the box. The SDK README says replies from Muse are text, shown as captions on boards with screens. To hear them, you send each reply to a text-to-speech API of your choice. The SDK points to start_tts in its source as the place to add it.

Do I need to know how to code to build one?

Not much. The SDK ships an AGENTS.md file that coding agents follow to build and flash the firmware, and Meta's Muse Code agent can do it while you approve each command. The Raspberry Pi path is one install script.

How much does a Muse gadget cost?

From $15 for a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (plus a power supply and microSD card) or $21.50 for an M5Stack StickS3, up to $99 for the color reTerminal E1002 on sale and $110 or more for a Raspberry Pi 5.

Can I sell Muse gadgets I build?

Not with a Muse SDK token inside. Meta's Gadget SDK terms say tokens are for personal, non-commercial use and can't go into a device you sell or list publicly without Meta's written permission. The SDK code itself is Apache 2.0.
