bodyHtml:
You can run Muse on a Raspberry Pi with Meta's Linux Device SDK. A small installer pairs the Pi with your Muse account over Bluetooth, and from then on Muse can run shell commands, read and write files, and check the machine's health. It isn't a talking speaker or a screen gadget. It gives your agent a Linux computer in your home to work on.

Quick answer

Any Raspberry Pi with Bluetooth works: a 3B+, 4, 5 or Zero 2 W. Get a Zero 2 W ($15) for light shell and file jobs, or a Pi 5 4GB ($110 list) if you want room for apps like Home Assistant. Add the right power supply and a microSD card, install Raspberry Pi OS, run Meta's install script with your SDK token, and pair in the Muse app. You don't need a mic, speaker or screen.

What Muse can do on a Raspberry Pi

The Linux Device SDK gives Muse four built-in commands:

  • system.run runs a shell command and returns its output and exit code.
  • file.read reads a file, 64 KB at a time.
  • file.write writes a file, 64 KB at a time, and replaces it only when the write is complete.
  • device.health reports uptime, load, memory, disk and temperature.

Commands run as the account you install the SDK for, with exactly that account's permissions. The README puts it plainly: "If it can use sudo, so can Muse." Meta's own example prompts include "What's using all the disk space on my Pi?" and "Install Home Assistant on my Pi and tell me how to open it."

It works the other way too. Any program on the Pi can send a message to Muse, with no credentials of its own, using a command like musegadget send-user-msg "The garage door has been open for an hour." The repo includes a full example that sends every note from a Pebble ring to its own Muse chat, and you can add your own commands in src/musegadget/executor.py.

Which Raspberry Pi to use

The SDK README lists the Raspberry Pi 3B+, 4, 5 and Zero 2 W. Here's how the most common choices compare. Prices are list prices, checked October 5, 2026.

ModelList priceCPU and memoryBluetoothPower inputBest for

Raspberry Pi 5 8GB$1752.4 GHz quad-core Cortex-A76, 8 GB5.0 / BLEUSB-C, 5 V 5 AHeavier apps, more headroom

Pi 5 prices went up in February and again in April 2026, following earlier rises Raspberry Pi said were "to offset the recent unprecedented rise in the cost of LPDDR4 memory". Resellers often charge more than list: the Walmart listing that gadgets.muse.ai links to was $199.99 for an 8GB board from a marketplace seller.

If you already own a Pi 4 or 3B+, use it. Other Linux computers work too if they have Bluetooth LE. hackshop's Zero 2 W page and Pi 5 page track current sellers.

What you need besides the board

  • A power supply. The Pi 5 needs 5 V at 5 A over USB-C with Power Delivery. Raspberry Pi's 27 W USB-C supply provides 5.1 V at 5 A. The Zero 2 W takes Micro USB at 5 V and 2.5 A, which Raspberry Pi's 12.5 W supply covers.
  • A microSD card. Raspberry Pi recommends at least 32 GB for Raspberry Pi OS with a desktop and at least 8 GB for Raspberry Pi OS Lite.
  • A supported OS. Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye or later, Debian 11 or later, or Ubuntu 22.04 or later, already on your network. 32-bit and 64-bit both work.
  • An account with sudo on the Pi.
  • An SDK token from gadgets.muse.ai (Account > SDK tokens). Every gadget needs one, including ones you build for yourself.
  • The Muse app on an iPhone or Android phone, to pair the device.

What you don't need: a microphone, a speaker or a screen. The Linux SDK has no voice or display features, so you talk to Muse in its app and Muse does the work on the Pi. You can even skip a monitor for setup, because Raspberry Pi Imager can set up networking, remote access and your login before the first boot. The hackshop store lists each part with seller links.

How to set up Muse on a Raspberry Pi

  1. Flash Raspberry Pi OS to the microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager. Set your Wi-Fi, username and SSH access in Imager so the Pi joins your network on first boot.
  2. Boot the Pi and log in, at the keyboard or over SSH.
  3. Create an SDK token at gadgets.muse.ai under Account > SDK tokens, and read the Gadget SDK Terms. Tokens start with mgst_.
  4. Download the installer with curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk/main/linux/install.sh -o install.sh, read it with less install.sh, then run it as the account Muse should use: bash install.sh --sdk-token mgst_YOUR_TOKEN. It installs into /opt/musegadget, starts the musegadget service, and asks before it gives Muse your account.
  5. In the Muse app, turn on Settings > Devices > Developer mode, then tap Add Device (the + icon). Pick the device named MuseGadgetXXXXXX. Muse warns that it's a community device. Continue if it's yours.
  6. When the app asks for Wi-Fi, pick the network shown. No password is needed because the Pi is already online.
  7. Ask Muse something simple, like "What's using all the disk space on my Pi?"

Pairing stays open for 10 minutes. If you miss it, run sudo musegadget pair. To check on the service, use sudo systemctl status musegadget, and to remove it, run bash install.sh --uninstall. hackshop's Raspberry Pi 5 build steps follow the same flow with a parts list.

Raspberry Pi vs an ESP32 board for Muse

Raspberry Pi (Linux SDK)ESP32 board (ESP32 SDK)
What Muse getsShell, file and health commandsStatus display, images, push-to-talk on full UI boards
VoiceNone built inPush-to-talk on boards with a mic
ScreenNot neededBuilt in on many boards
SetupInstall script, no flashingBuild and flash firmware with ESP-IDF 6.0.1 from a Mac or Linux computer
Starting price$15 (Zero 2 W) plus power supply and card$21.50 (M5Stack StickS3)
AccessYour account's permissions, sudo includedOnly the commands the firmware offers

The Pi wins when you want Muse to do real work: manage files, check backups or look after Home Assistant. An ESP32 board wins when you want something to hold and talk to. You can have both: pair a Pi and a small voice board like the M5Stack StickS3 with the same account, since one SDK token can be linked to up to 50 devices.

Keep it safe

  • Limit the account. Muse gets the same access as the account you install it for. Run bash install.sh --run-as someone to give Muse a different account, such as one without sudo.
  • Pair on a network you trust. Pairing only opens when you run the installer or musegadget pair on the machine. It has no manufacturer verification and can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack.
  • Know where the token lives. It's saved in /var/lib/musegadget/sdk_token, readable only by root.
  • Don't build anything critical on it. Meta says the SDK and tokens are not a supported product and may change, stop working or be withdrawn at any time.

The Linux SDK README lists the Raspberry Pi 3B+, 4, 5 and Zero 2 W. Other Linux computers work too if they have Bluetooth LE and run Debian 11 or later or Ubuntu 22.04 or later.

Do I need a monitor and keyboard?

No. Raspberry Pi Imager can set up networking, remote access and your login before the first boot, so you can do the whole install over SSH.

Is it safe to let Muse use sudo?

That's your call. Muse gets exactly the permissions of the account you install it for, so if that account can use sudo, so can Muse. To limit it, run the installer with --run-as and pick an account without sudo.

For a Muse desk companion, the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C is the best all-round pick, the Seeed SenseCAP Watcher is the one to buy if you want a camera, and the AIPI Lite is the cheapest. All three run the Muse ESP32 SDK's full on-screen UI: an animated avatar, push-to-talk and settings. The real differences are the screen, the camera and how hard the first flash is.

Quick answer

Buy the Waveshare 1.75C ($39.99, or $41.99 with a battery) for the best screen and an easy flash. Buy the SenseCAP Watcher ($60.99) if you want Muse to take photos and don't mind a slow, fussy first flash. Buy the AIPI Lite ($35.99) if you want a small battery-powered buddy and can live with a 128×128 screen.

Watcher vs Waveshare vs AIPI Lite at a glance

Prices are from each seller's US page, checked October 5, 2026. Specs come from the sellers and the Muse SDK's device table.

Seeed SenseCAP WatcherWaveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75CAIPI Lite

First flashHard: backup, two ports, about 3 minutesEasy: chip's own USBEasy: chip's own USB

All three show images Muse sends, run the home-network tunnel, report battery status and get over-the-air updates.

Screen and voice

The Waveshare's 1.75-inch AMOLED is the largest and highest-resolution screen of the three, at 466×466, and it sits in a CNC aluminum case. The Watcher's 1.45-inch 412×412 round LCD is close behind. It's also the screen Meta's desktop simulator copies, so UI previews on your computer match a Watcher. The AIPI Lite's 128×128 screen is small: during pairing it even leaves out the device name and state because there's no room.

Voice works the same way on all three. You press a button and talk, the board sends your voice note, and Muse transcribes it and answers in writing. The answer shows as captions. Meta's project card says the AIPI Lite "answers out loud", but the SDK README says replies are text and spoken answers need a text-to-speech API you add at the start_tts hook. Plan on reading captions unless you set that up. Waveshare says its dual-mic array is built for noise reduction and echo cancellation.

Camera: only the Watcher has one

The SenseCAP Watcher is the only board in the Muse SDK with camera support. Seeed builds it around an ESP32-S3 plus a Himax WiseEye2 HX6538 AI chip and a camera.

  • The camera is off by default. Turn on "SenseCAP Watcher camera capture and live preview" (CONFIG_MUSE_WATCHER_CAMERA=y) under Muse in menuconfig, then rebuild.
  • Double-click the wheel to open a live view, then tap TAP TO TAKE PHOTO or double-click again.
  • Muse can call camera.capture, which returns a JPEG. A capture takes under a second, and the camera only has power while a capture or the live view runs.
  • Photo attachments to voice messages are not included.

How hard is each one to flash?

All three need a USB data cable, a Mac or Linux computer, ESP-IDF version 6.0.1 and your SDK token. Muse Code, or any coding agent that reads the SDK's AGENTS.md, can run the build and flash for you. The Waveshare and the AIPI Lite both use the ESP32-S3's own USB port, so you build with the board's settings file and flash as usual. The AIPI Lite doesn't come with a USB-C cable, so buy a data cable with it.

The Watcher takes more care:

  1. Back up its factory data. Muse overwrites the Watcher's nvsfactory partition at 0x9000, which is unique to each unit. Save it with tools/muse/paced_esptool.py --chip esp32s3 -p PORT read-flash 0x9000 0x32000 nvsfactory.bin. You need that file to go back to Seeed's firmware.
  2. Pick the right port. The bottom USB-C has a CH342 bridge that shows up as two ports. The ESP32-S3 console is the second one, ending in 3. The first is the Himax camera chip. The ESP32 port finder helps you tell them apart.
  3. Flash with the paced tool. Use tools/muse/board.sh flash watcher, which sends 64 bytes at a time at 115200 baud. Plain esptool fails on this bridge with "0107: Checksum error" or "0105: The format of the received message is invalid". A lower baud or another USB port doesn't help. On macOS you don't need WCH's driver.
  4. Wait. The flash shows nothing for about three minutes. Don't interrupt it, or the board won't boot until a flash succeeds.

If plain esptool already failed, the Watcher isn't bricked. The failed write erased the bootloader, but the ROM loader still answers, and a paced flash fixes it. One more difference: putting your own avatar on a Watcher takes the manual steps in the SDK's avatar recipe instead of the one-command tool. hackshop's Watcher build steps cover the whole sequence.

Which Muse desk companion should you buy?

  • Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C if you want the best-looking desk object and the easiest setup. Get the $41.99 version, which comes with a battery that fits inside the case, if you'll move it around. Meta lists it as an example project. See the Waveshare board page.
  • Seeed SenseCAP Watcher if you want Muse to see. It's the only one with a camera, and the wheel is a handy control. Budget extra time for the backup and the slow first flash. See the Watcher board page.
  • AIPI Lite if price and portability matter most. It's $35.99 with a 450 mAh battery module, but the screen is tiny and it needs 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. AIPI sells its own optional plans (Pro is $9.99 a month), and they're separate from Muse. See the AIPI Lite board page.

If none of these fit, two other boards are worth a look. The M5Stack StickS3 ($21.50) is cheaper and fits in a pocket. The Waveshare ESP32-C6-Touch-AMOLED-1.8 has a bigger screen but no PSRAM, so replies scroll past as text and it can't show images.

The Waveshare 1.75C and the AIPI Lite. Both flash over the ESP32-S3's own USB port with the normal build and flash steps. The SenseCAP Watcher needs a factory-data backup, the right one of two ports and a paced flash that shows nothing for about three minutes.

Can the SenseCAP Watcher send photos to Muse?

Yes, once you turn on the camera build option. Muse can call camera.capture, which returns a JPEG, and you can open a live view by double-clicking the wheel. Photos can't be attached to voice messages.

Do these boards speak Muse's replies?

Not out of the box. Muse answers in text, which shows as captions on the screen. To hear replies, you connect a text-to-speech API at the start_tts hook in the SDK source.

Did I brick my Watcher if esptool failed?

No. Plain esptool erases the bootloader before it fails on the Watcher's USB bridge, so the board won't boot, but the ROM loader still answers. Flash again with tools/muse/board.sh flash watcher and let it finish.

bodyHtml:
A Muse family calendar on e-paper is a Seeed reTerminal E1001 or E1002 running Meta's ESP32 Device SDK, placed where everyone walks past. Muse sends it a picture, such as this week's schedule, a chore chart or a shopping list, and the e-paper keeps showing it with no power. It's a quiet, slow, low-power status board. It isn't a tablet, and it doesn't take voice.

Quick answer

Get the reTerminal E1001 ($69 on sale, regular $79) for a black and white calendar that refreshes in a second or two. Get the E1002 ($99 on sale, regular $109) for six colors, with a refresh that takes about 30 seconds and flashes. Flash the matching Muse build, pair it in the Muse app, and ask Muse to send a calendar image. Expect still pictures only: no video, no touch and no voice.

What a Muse family calendar can show

Out of the box, both reTerminals show a still status screen with your agent's name, its character and a line of status text. It only changes when the status does. The useful part is images. Muse can send the board a picture, and the board dithers it to what the panel can show:

  • The E1001 shows black and white only, 1 bit per pixel.
  • The E1002 shows six inks: black, white, yellow, red, blue and green. Grays become black and white.

Both panels are 800×480. The firmware's display.draw_url command tells Muse the bit depth, and on the E1002 the six exact colors and how slow the refresh is, so Muse can draw for the screen it has. Meta suggests the E1002 for "a morning briefing, reminders, shopping list, or anything else you think of." A family calendar is the same idea: Muse draws the week as an image and sends it.

What goes on the calendar depends on what Muse can see. If your family's events aren't somewhere Muse can read, tell it what's coming up and ask it to draw that. Meta's example prompts for gadgets include daily jobs such as "Every morning at 7, check if my Pi's backups ran", so a fresh page each morning is a reasonable thing to ask for.

E1001 vs E1002 for a family calendar

For a calendar that changes several times a day, the E1001 is the practical pick. Text is what matters, and a quick refresh means a fixed typo or a moved pickup shows up fast. Pick the E1002 if color coding matters to your family, such as a color per person, and you're fine with each update taking half a minute. Board details live on the E1001 page and the E1002 page.

What to expect from e-paper

  • Slow refresh. A second or two on the E1001, about 30 seconds on the E1002. Both flash briefly when the image changes.
  • No video or animation. At that speed, e-paper is for still pages.
  • It holds the picture with no power. The SDK notes say the E1001 keeps its picture without power, and the E1002 is the same board with a color panel.
  • Low power, with a caveat. Seeed advertises up to three months of battery life and lists a 2000 mAh battery for the E1001. The Muse firmware keeps an encrypted session to Muse, and the repo gives no battery figure for it, so see how long yours lasts before you rely on the battery alone. Muse can't read the battery level on these boards either.
  • No voice and no touch. The reTerminals have no push-to-talk under Muse. You talk to Muse in the app or through a separate voice gadget.
  • Some hardware sits idle. Seeed's board has temperature and humidity sensors and a buzzer, but the Muse SDK lists air-sensor support only for the SenseCAP Indicator, so don't count on Muse reading them here.
  • Updates go over USB. Over-the-air updates are off on these boards by default, so reflashing means plugging in a cable.

Wall, fridge or desk: where to put it

Seeed's E1001 wiki says a 3D-printed stand comes in the package. It attaches to embedded nuts on the bottom back and holds the screen at a fixed angle. With the stand, the E1001 measures 176 × 120 × 53 mm, and it's 17 mm thick without it. That works on a kitchen counter or a desk.

For a wall or fridge, plan your own mount. Seeed doesn't list magnets, so a fridge needs adhesive magnets or a printed bracket, and a wall works with a small shelf or a bracket that uses the same screw inserts. Browse hackshop's templates for printable stands you can start from. A few placement tips:

  • Stay in range of your 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. The ESP32-S3 inside uses 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n.
  • Leave the top edge clear. The buttons, including the green one you press during pairing, are on top.
  • Keep a USB-C cable within reach. The port charges at 5 V 1 A and is also how you flash the board.
  • Pick a spot at eye level where people already stop, like the fridge, the front door or the kitchen table.

How to set it up

  1. Get the board and a USB-C cable that carries data. Charge-only cables can't flash.
  2. Create an SDK token at gadgets.muse.ai under Account > SDK tokens.
  3. On a Mac or Linux computer, install ESP-IDF version 6.0.1. The Muse firmware doesn't support other versions, including the newer 6.1.
  4. Clone the muse-gadget-sdk repo and build with tools/board.sh reterminal-e1001 build or tools/board.sh reterminal-e1002 build, with your token set for that build in idf.py menuconfig (under ESP32 Device SDK). Use the E1002 build for the color panel, even though the "Source" link on Meta's E1002 project card points to the E1001 settings file.
  5. Flash it. The reTerminal uses a CH340 USB bridge, so the port shows up as /dev/cu.usbserial-* or /dev/cu.wchusbserial* on a Mac and /dev/ttyUSB* on Linux. On Linux, add yourself to the dialout group first.
  6. In the Muse app, turn on Settings > Devices > Developer mode and add the device. It shows up as MuseGadget-Disp-XXXXXX. Press the green button when asked to confirm.
  7. Ask Muse for a first page, such as "Draw this week's family calendar in large black and white text and send it to my e-paper display."

You can hand the build to a coding agent instead. Muse Code, or any agent that reads the SDK's AGENTS.md, can build and flash it, and hackshop's E1001 build steps include a brief your agent can follow. If you can't tell which port is the board, try the ESP32 port finder.

Questions people ask

How often can a Muse e-paper calendar update?

As often as Muse sends a new image, but each refresh takes time: a second or two on the E1001, and about 30 seconds with a flash on the E1002. Plan for a few updates a day, not live data.

Does the reTerminal run on battery with Muse?

Both reTerminals have a battery, and Seeed advertises up to three months of battery life. The Muse repo gives no battery figure for its firmware, and Muse can't read the battery level on these boards, so check it yourself and keep a USB-C cable handy.

Can my family talk to the calendar?

No. The reTerminal has no push-to-talk under the Muse firmware. You ask Muse in the Muse app, or through a separate voice gadget, and Muse updates the screen. The board is paired to one Muse account.

Should I get the E1001 or E1002 for a fridge?

The E1001 if your calendar changes often and is mostly text: it's cheaper and refreshes in a second or two. The E1002 if color coding matters and a 30-second refresh is fine. Seeed doesn't list magnets for either, so plan your own mount.

bodyHtml:
Here's what Muse Gadgets can do: show Muse's status on a light or screen, display images Muse sends, take push-to-talk voice notes, take photos on one board, and run shell commands on a Raspberry Pi. They can't speak replies without extra work, go into a product you sell, or count on Meta for support. The code is open source, but the tokens that connect gadgets to Muse have their own terms.

Quick answer

Muse Gadgets come in three tiers: status boards (a light, LED ring, screen or e-paper), full UI boards (avatar, push-to-talk, settings and usually images) and Linux boxes (shell, files and health). Voice is push-to-talk, and replies come back as text. Only the SenseCAP Watcher supports a camera. You need the Muse app on iOS or Android and an SDK token. Tokens are for personal, non-commercial use, top out at 50 devices, and can't go into a device you sell.

What Muse Gadgets can do, tier by tier

TierExample boardsWhat you getWhat you don't
Status lightESP32-C5 DevKitC-1, ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1A status light and a buttonScreen, images, voice
Status screen or e-paperideaspark 1.9", SenseCAP Indicator, reTerminal E1001 and E1002Status on a screen, images from MuseVoice, on-screen settings
Voice with an LED ringHome Assistant Voice Preview EditionPush-to-talk, status on the ring, volume dialReplies on the device (they show in the Muse app)
Full UIWaveshare 1.75C, AIPI Lite, SenseCAP Watcher, M5Stack StickS3Animated avatar, push-to-talk, settings, images on most boardsSpoken replies without your own text-to-speech
LinuxRaspberry Pi 3B+, 4, 5 and Zero 2 WShell commands, file read and write, health reportsVoice or a screen UI

Boards with PSRAM also run the home-network tunnel, which lets Muse reach devices you already own and anything you build with a local HTTP API. Boards without PSRAM, like the classic ESP32 and the ESP32-C6, skip it. You can also give Muse new commands of your own on both SDKs. Check a board you own with Does my board run Muse?, or compare them all in the Muse board guide.

Voice, screens and camera: the details

Voice

Voice input is push-to-talk. You press a button, the board sends a voice note, and Muse transcribes it and answers in writing. Boards with a screen show the answer as captions; on the Home Assistant Voice PE, replies show up in the Muse app. For spoken answers, you send each reply to a text-to-speech API of your choice at the SDK's start_tts hook.

Screens and images

Most full UI boards and several status boards show pictures Muse sends. E-paper is slow: a second or two per refresh on the reTerminal E1001, and about 30 seconds on the color E1002. Some boards without PSRAM, like the Waveshare C6 1.8, can't show images and get replies as scrolling text.

Camera

The Seeed SenseCAP Watcher is the only board with camera support, and it's off by default. Turn on CONFIG_MUSE_WATCHER_CAMERA=y and rebuild, and Muse can call camera.capture to get a JPEG. Photo attachments to voice messages are not included, and other boards' cameras, like the M5Stack CoreS3's, aren't used yet. The Watcher board page has the details.

What you need: account, app and computer

  • Muse. It's rolling out in the US, and Meta says it's "free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more".
  • The Muse app on iOS or Android. Gadgets pair under Settings > Devices with Developer mode on, and show up with a "MuseGadget" prefix.
  • An SDK token. Get one at gadgets.muse.ai under Account > SDK tokens. Every gadget needs one to pair, including ones you build for yourself.
  • For ESP32 boards: a USB cable that carries data, a computer running macOS or Linux, and ESP-IDF version 6.0.1. Other versions aren't supported.
  • For a Linux box: Bluetooth LE, Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye, Debian 11 or Ubuntu 22.04 (or later), and an account with sudo.

The SDK READMEs don't list a paid Muse plan as a requirement. Muse Home Link, Meta's own Wi-Fi gadget, is different: it's "Free with an active Muse subscription in the United States only, limit one per subscriber," and "Claiming holds your place in line; it isn't an order." The page doesn't say whether the free tier counts.

Limits and risks to know

  • It's a hobby project. Meta's page warns that side effects of tinkering "may include bricked boards, voided warranties, brownouts, or bankruptcies."
  • Pairing isn't verified. The SDK says pairing "has no manufacturer verification and can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack." Set gadgets up on a network you trust.
  • Your token ships in the firmware. Treat it as an identifier, not a password, and revoke it if it leaks. Meta also "strongly recommend[s] enabling NVS encryption" so stored Wi-Fi credentials can't be read off the board.
  • Linux gadgets get real access. Muse runs commands with the permissions of the account you install it for. In the README's words, "If it can use sudo, so can Muse."
  • Keep boards reflashable. Don't enable Secure Boot, flash encryption or CONFIG_HOMEHUB_PAIRING_EFUSE_AUTH on a board you want to keep reflashing.
  • The hardware isn't Meta's. "Devices shown here are made and sold by other companies, and Meta doesn't endorse or warrant them."

More in the home network security guide.

Muse Gadget SDK terms: the key points

The token terms are at gadgets.muse.ai/sdk-terms. Read them in full before you share a device. This summary quotes them where the wording matters, and it isn't legal advice.

  • Permitted use. Tokens are "for personal, non-commercial use with your own Muse account and for devices you build and share" under the terms' device-sharing section.
  • Device limits. "You may embed it in no more than 50 devices that you make available to others. A Token may be linked to no more than 50 total devices."
  • No selling. A token may not go into a device "that you sell for any payment or other consideration, that you advertise, offer, or list publicly or through any marketplace or application store", or one that's part of a promotion or reward.
  • Other distribution. "Any other distribution requires Meta's prior written permission." You also may not imply that Meta made or endorsed the device.
  • Other people's data. If you give a device to someone else, you must tell them what it does with their information before they pair it, and you may not keep or reuse their prompts or data.
  • No support. The SDK and tokens "are not a supported product and not a developer platform. They may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time".
  • Revocation. Meta may revoke a token. After that, you must "remove the Token from any device you have made available to others".
  • Code vs tokens. The code is Apache 2.0, but "The source code license does not grant any right to Gadget SDK Tokens."

The code license has exceptions too: the bundled minimp3 decoder is CC0-1.0, pixel_font.c is BSD-2-Clause, and "The Apache License does not cover the Jollybot avatar."

What the terms mean for your build

  • A gadget for yourself: this is the personal, non-commercial use the terms describe.
  • A gadget for family or a friend: allowed within the 50-device limits, if you tell them what it does with their information before they pair it.
  • Kits or finished gadgets for sale with a token inside: not allowed without Meta's written permission.
  • Forking or selling the code: Apache 2.0 allows it, commercial use included, as long as you keep the license and notices. The limit is on Muse-connected devices, not the code.

More on licenses in open source vs closed AI hardware.

Questions people ask

Can I sell a Muse gadget I built?

Not with a Muse SDK token inside. The terms bar tokens in any device you sell, advertise or list publicly, and any other distribution needs Meta's prior written permission. The SDK code itself is Apache 2.0, so you can fork it and sell your own code.

How many devices can one SDK token pair with?

A token may be linked to no more than 50 devices in total, and you may embed it in no more than 50 devices that you make available to others.

Do Muse gadgets need a paid Muse subscription?

The SDK READMEs list the Muse app, an SDK token and the hardware, not a paid plan. Muse Home Link is different: Meta offers it free with an active Muse subscription in the United States only, one per subscriber.

Can Muse gadgets talk back?

Not by default. Replies are text, shown as captions or in the Muse app. You can add spoken replies with a text-to-speech API at the SDK's start_tts hook.

bodyHtml:
Build vs buy an AI gadget? It comes down to control versus convenience. Build your own if you want a device that does exactly what you choose, costs $21.50 to $69 for the board, and stays yours to fix and reflash. Buy a finished one if it has to work out of the box for people who will never open a terminal, and you accept that the maker decides what it does and how long it lasts.

Quick answer

For most people who want to give Muse a body, building is the practical choice today, because Meta's own Muse hardware is limited. Home Link is free with an active Muse subscription in the US only, one per subscriber. The TV stick is marked coming soon, and the pocket-sized Muse Charm has no price yet. Build if you have a few hours and a USB data cable. Buy if the device is for someone who needs it to just work.

What building and buying mean for AI gadgets

Building, here, does not mean designing a circuit board. In Meta's words, "Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself." You take an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or a Raspberry Pi, install Meta's open source firmware or Linux SDK, and pair it with the Muse app. None of the boards in the Muse board guide need soldering for the basic build.

Buying means a finished product: hardware, firmware and service in one package, with the company handling updates. Some products sit in between. The AIPI Lite is sold as a finished voice gadget, yet it runs on an "ESP32-S3 with hackable firmware" and is on Meta's supported list.

Meta's own Muse hardware: what you can buy or claim

  • Muse Home Link. It lets you "connect Muse to your home Wi-Fi so it can reach compatible devices you already own, or anything you build with a local HTTP API." It is free with an active Muse subscription, US only, one per subscriber, shipping in October. "Claiming holds your place in line; it isn't an order." Engadget reported 5,000 units; Meta's page gives no count.
  • Muse on your TV. An HDMI stick so Muse can put things on the big screen. Marked "coming soon," with no price.
  • Muse Charm. A "pocket-sized device" with real-time voice, previewed at Connect 2026. No price yet.
  • Glasses. Ray-Ban Meta Audio from $349, Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 from $449 and Meta Adventurer from $249. Meta says they connect to Muse.

Notice what is missing: a finished Muse device for your desk with a screen, a push-to-talk remote, or an e-paper wall display. Home Link is a bridge, not a body. It helps Muse reach things on your network, including a gadget you build. For those other forms, you build.

Build vs buy an AI gadget at a glance

FactorBuild your ownBuy a finished device
Upfront cost$21.50 (M5Stack StickS3) to $69 (Home Assistant Voice PE) for an ESP32 board, plus a data cableHome Link free with an active Muse subscription (US). Muse-ready glasses from $249. Muse Charm unpriced.
Time to first useAbout 1 to 3 hours on hackshop's estimatesMinutes
FlexibilityChange firmware, add sensors, write your own commandsWhat the maker ships, plus settings
SupportNo warranty. The SDK is "not a supported product." Docs, your agent and the community Discord.Usually a warranty and a support channel
RepairabilityOff-the-shelf parts you can swapDepends on the maker
If the company changes plansFirmware and code stay with you. The Muse link depends on Meta's tokens.The device can stop working, as the Humane AI Pin did
Best forTinkerers and the curiousPeople who want it to just work

Cost: what you actually spend

Board prices, checked October 5, 2026:

  • M5Stack StickS3: $21.50, with speaker, mic and battery.
  • AIPI Lite: $35.99, with a 450 mAh battery module but no USB-C cable or power adapter.
  • Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C: $39.99 to $41.99, depending on the battery option.
  • Seeed SenseCAP Watcher W1-A: $60.99, with a camera.
  • Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition: $69 recommended MSRP.
  • Raspberry Pi 5: $110 for 4GB and $175 for 8GB at list price. Third-party listings run higher.

Add a USB cable that carries data, not just power. A printed stand is optional, and you can get one printed without owning a printer. The hackshop store page lists every part with seller links, and you always do the checkout yourself.

The buy side has hidden costs too. Home Link needs an active Muse subscription, and Meta's announcement gives no plan prices. Some gadgets sell their own plans: AIPI lists Pro at $9.99 a month, separate from Muse.

Time, support and repairability

Time

hackshop's build pages estimate one to three hours of setup for most ESP32 boards. Most of that is installing tools and waiting for the first build. The flash itself can take just seconds, though a SenseCAP Watcher flash "shows nothing for about three minutes." You do not have to type every command. Meta's README says any coding agent that reads the repo's AGENTS.md can build and flash.

Support

This is the honest weak spot of building. Meta's terms say the SDK and tokens "are not a supported product and not a developer platform. They may change, stop working, or be withdrawn at any time." The firmware is "provided as-is, without warranty." Your help desk is the docs, your agent and the community Discord.

Repairability and longevity

When you build, every part is replaceable, and Muse builds never turn on Secure Boot, "so you can reflash your board as often as you like." Raspberry Pi says the Pi 5 stays in production until at least January 2036. Check that your board is still sold, though: the M5Stack StickC Plus2 is listed as end of life.

Finished devices last as long as their maker supports them. The FTC's 2021 "Nixing the Fix" report found "scant evidence to support manufacturers' justifications for repair restrictions." The Humane AI Pin shows the bigger risk: after HP bought Humane's assets for $116 million, the Pin shut down on February 28, 2025, and its AI queries, calls and texts stopped working. Building does not remove this risk completely, since Meta can revoke tokens. But your board still works, and you can flash something else onto it.

Who should build and who should buy

Build if

  • You want a form Meta does not sell: a desk companion, a pocket push-to-talk remote, a wall display or a hidden Linux box.
  • You enjoy tinkering, or want to learn while an agent does the typing.
  • You want to add sensors or your own voice. Muse replies arrive as text; spoken replies need your own text-to-speech API.

Buy if

  • The device is for someone who will never update firmware.
  • You need a warranty and support you can call.
  • You only need Muse to reach devices you already own. Home Link is built for that.

The middle path

Buy a finished device that is also hackable, then flash it. The AIPI Lite and the Waveshare round AMOLED are complete, cased products that run Muse's full on-screen UI. Read each board's notes first: on the Home Assistant Voice PE you flash the ESP32-S3 only and "never reflash" the XMOS audio chip. Not sure which fits? The Muse board picker asks four questions and suggests three boards.

Questions people ask

Is it cheaper to build an AI gadget than to buy one?

Usually, for the hardware. A Muse-ready board costs $21.50 to $69, plus a data cable. Meta's own Muse hardware is free with a subscription (Home Link), unpriced (Muse Charm) or not out yet (the TV stick). The real cost of building is your time and the lack of formal support.

Can I buy a ready-made Muse gadget?

Meta does not sell a finished Muse desk gadget yet. It offers Home Link, free with an active Muse subscription in the US, and glasses that connect to Muse. Devices like the AIPI Lite are finished products you can flash with Muse firmware yourself.

Do I need to know how to code to build one?

No. A coding agent can run the commands for you; Meta's README says any agent that reads AGENTS.md can build and flash. You plug in the cable, press a button if asked, and pair in the Muse app.

What happens to my build if Meta stops supporting the SDK?

The Muse connection would stop, since Meta says the SDK and tokens may be withdrawn at any time. The board still works, and because Muse builds never turn on Secure Boot, you can flash other firmware onto it.

bodyHtml:
Open source vs closed AI hardware is not a yes-or-no question. Every AI gadget has layers: the board design, the firmware, the SDK, the cloud service and the agent itself, and each one can be open or closed on its own. In Muse Gadgets, Meta publishes the device firmware and SDKs under the Apache 2.0 license, the boards come from other companies, and the Muse service and its access tokens stay under Meta's control.

Quick answer

Ask which layers are open, not whether the product is. With Muse Gadgets you can read, change and reflash the device code, but talking to Muse needs a revocable, non-commercial SDK token. hackshop's planner and MCP server are free and MIT-licensed. Open layers give you control, repairability and a longer hardware life. Closed layers usually give you polish, a warranty and automatic updates.

What "open source hardware" means

The Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA) defines it this way: "Open source hardware is hardware whose design is made publicly available so that anyone can study, modify, distribute, make, and sell the design or hardware based on that design." The full definition has 12 criteria, including documentation, necessary software, derived works, free redistribution and attribution.

OSHWA also runs a certification. It is self-certification under a license agreement that lets a maker use the Open Source Hardware Certification logo, and it lasts one year before it is reaffirmed.

By that standard, "open" means design files you can build from. Some products called open publish only their software and firmware. That is narrower, not dishonest. When you see the word, check which layer it covers.

The five layers of an AI gadget

1. Board hardware and schematics

For Muse gadgets, the boards are off-the-shelf products. Meta's page says they "are made and sold by other companies, and Meta doesn't endorse or warrant them." Whether a board's schematics are published depends on its maker, so check the vendor's page. Some go all the way: Home Assistant advertises its Voice Preview Edition as "Fully open software, firmware, and hardware."

2. Firmware

Meta's Muse device firmware is open source under Apache 2.0, with listed exceptions: minimp3 is CC0-1.0, pixel_font.c is BSD-2-Clause, and "The Apache License does not cover the Jollybot avatar." Muse builds never turn on Secure Boot, "so you can reflash your board as often as you like." Flashing Muse replaces the vendor's firmware, so back up first where the SDK says to.

3. SDK and developer code

The ESP32 and Linux SDKs live in Meta's public muse-gadget-sdk repository, each with a README and an AGENTS.md for coding agents. Apache 2.0 grants a "perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, no-charge, royalty-free, irrevocable copyright license" to reproduce, modify and distribute the code, commercial use included, as long as you keep the license and notices and mark changed files.

4. Cloud service and access

This is where Muse Gadgets is closed. Every gadget needs an SDK token to pair, and tokens sit under separate terms: "personal, non-commercial use," no more than 50 devices per token, and no token in a device you sell or list on a marketplace. Meta can revoke a token, and "The source code license does not grant any right to Gadget SDK Tokens." You can fork and sell the code, but not a Muse-connected device, without Meta's written permission.

5. The agent itself

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, powered by its Muse Spark model, and it runs as Meta's service. The SDK connects your device to it; it does not include it. Muse replies arrive as text, and spoken replies need your own text-to-speech API, hooked in at start_tts in the firmware source.

Open source vs closed AI hardware: what is open where

AgentMuse, run by MetaYour choice of agent that speaks MCPVendor's assistant

What hackshop opens, and what it does not

hackshop is free and open source. Its code, including the build planner, the MCP server and the board catalog, is public on GitHub under the MIT license. Your agent can use the hosted MCP server at https://www.hackshop.dev/mcp or run the hackshop-mcp npm package locally. The printable desk stands on build pages, such as the Waveshare round AMOLED build, come as STL and STEP files you can print anywhere.

hackshop does not change what Meta opens or keeps closed. Your gadget still needs Meta's SDK token under Meta's terms. hackshop does not make boards, and it never buys anything without your OK. Agents can read agents.md for how to use it.

The tradeoffs: control, longevity, support, polish and security

Control

Open firmware and SDKs let you add sensors, change the screen, write commands and choose your own speech service. The Linux SDK includes a shell command, and its README is blunt: "If it can use sudo, so can Muse." Control comes with responsibility.

Longevity

Closed devices live and die with their company. The Humane AI Pin shut down on February 28, 2025, after HP bought Humane's assets for $116 million, and its AI queries, calls and texts stopped working. Open firmware protects the hardware, not the service. If Meta withdrew Muse tokens, your gadget would lose its Muse link, but you could reflash the board for another project.

Support

Closed products usually come with a warranty. Meta says the SDK and tokens "are not a supported product and not a developer platform," and the code is "provided as-is, without warranty." Plan on helping yourself, with your agent and the community.

Polish

A closed product is designed as one object. A DIY build has rough edges. You may want a printed stand, and a refresh on the six-color reTerminal E1002 "takes about 30 seconds and flashes."

Security updates

A closed vendor pushes updates to you until it stops. With open firmware, you pull updates and reflash; Muse's over-the-air updates are off by default except on boards with the full UI. Pairing "has no manufacturer verification and can't prevent an active man-in-the-middle attack," so set it up on a network you trust. Treat the token "as an identifier rather than a password," and turn on NVS encryption, as the README strongly recommends. Meta also says never to enable Secure Boot or flash encryption on a board you want to keep reflashing. Easy to reflash means easy for anyone holding the board to reflash, too.

How to choose

  • Want to change how the device behaves? You need open firmware and an open SDK.
  • Want to make your own boards? You need open design files, the layer OSHWA certifies.
  • Accept a closed layer where it buys you something. Muse runs as Meta's service, which is why a $21.50 board can talk to it.
  • Read the terms of every closed layer. For Muse, that means the 50-device cap, no selling and revocable tokens.
  • Prefer hardware you can repurpose. A board you can reflash outlives any one service.

To compare boards by what they can do, see the Muse board guide.

Questions people ask

bodyHtml:
Can you do hardware if you have never done it before? Yes, if your first hardware project is the right one. A good first hardware project for beginners uses a board that works as-is, needs no soldering, and loads its software over a USB cable. Turning an ESP32 board into a body for your AI agent fits: you need a data cable, a few Terminal commands your agent can run for you, and patience while it flashes.

Quick answer

Start with a board Meta's Muse SDK supports, such as the Espressif ESP32-C5-DevKitC-1 (Muse's suggested quickest start) or a complete device like the AIPI Lite ($35.99). Use a USB cable that carries data, find the right serial port, never unplug the board mid-flash, and back up stock firmware on boards that need it. Let your coding agent run the commands while you watch.

The skills a first hardware project actually needs

Fewer than you think. Meta's ESP32 SDK lists five requirements: an ESP32 board, "a USB cable that carries data, not just power," a computer running macOS or Linux, an SDK token and the Muse app. In skills, that means:

  • Using the right cable. Many of these boards use USB-C, and the cable must carry data. Plenty of cables only charge.
  • Running commands, or letting your agent do it. The manual path is idf.py menuconfig to set your token, idf.py build, and idf.py -p PORT flash monitor. A coding agent can run all three.
  • Patience while flashing. Writing the firmware can take just seconds; Espressif's sample log shows about three seconds of write time. Installing the tools and the first build take far longer. Some boards are slow: a SenseCAP Watcher flash "shows nothing for about three minutes."
  • Reading a status light. Orange breathing means ready for setup, blue breathing means press the button, green means connected, purple means not paired, and red blinking means an error.

What you do not need: soldering, electronics theory or a 3D printer. A printed stand is a nice extra later.

The easiest boards to start with

These boards are on Meta's supported list and in hackshop's Muse board guide. Prices checked October 5, 2026.

BoardPriceWhy it is a good first boardWatch out for
Espressif ESP32-C5-DevKitC-1Varies by sellerMuse's suggested quickest start; it "works as-is with its built-in status light and BOOT button"No screen or voice, status light only
AIPI Lite$35.99Complete palm-size device with the full on-screen UI, push-to-talk and a 450 mAh battery moduleNo USB-C cable or power adapter in the box; needs 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi
Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75C$39.99 to $41.99Round touch AMOLED in an aluminum case, full UIPrice depends on the battery option
M5Stack StickS3$21.50Cheapest full-UI board here, with speaker, mic and batteryFirst flash needs a workaround: it ships with UiFlow2, which switches off USB serial, and it has no BOOT button
Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W$15The Linux SDK installs like regular software and runs as a serviceNeeds Raspberry Pi OS, power and storage set up first

Save these for your second project: the SenseCAP Watcher (back up its factory partition, pick the right one of two ports, wait out a silent three-minute flash), the Home Assistant Voice PE (flash the ESP32-S3 only and "never reflash" the XMOS audio chip), and the StickC Plus2, which is end of life. For a pick based on your goals, try the Muse board picker.

Common first-timer mistakes

  1. Using a charge-only cable. Arduino's support page says to connect "with a data USB cable, not a charging-only cable." Espressif's guide also reminds you that some dev boards use USB-C and need the correct cable. If no port appears, try another cable first. The AIPI Lite does not include one, so buy it with the board.
  2. Picking the wrong serial port. Boards with the chip's own USB (C5, C6, S3) show up as /dev/cu.usbmodem* on macOS or /dev/ttyACM* on Linux. CH340 bridge boards, like the ideaspark and reTerminal, show up as /dev/cu.usbserial-*, /dev/cu.wchusbserial* or /dev/ttyUSB*. The Watcher shows two ports, and the ESP32-S3 is the second one, ending in 3. Unplug and replug to see which entry appears, or use the ESP32 port finder.
  3. Leaving the port open in another app. esptool's guide says to make sure no other software, such as a serial terminal, has the port open.
  4. Skipping the Linux permission step. If you see "Permission denied," run sudo usermod -a -G dialout $USER, then log out and back in.
  5. Interrupting a flash. Espressif warns: "Do not disconnect your device while the flash erasing is in progress." An interrupted Watcher flash leaves the board unable to boot until a flash succeeds. It is not bricked; you flash again.
  6. Not backing up. On the Watcher, Muse overwrites factory data unique to each unit, so back up its nvsfactory partition first. On the StickS3, back up the full 8 MB flash if you might want UiFlow2 back.
  7. Installing the wrong ESP-IDF. Muse needs ESP-IDF "version 6.0.1. Other versions aren't supported." Espressif's stable docs now show 6.1, so do not just grab the latest.

If flashing cannot connect at all: "hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT, and try again." Reflashing keeps your pairing and Wi-Fi settings.

How your agent can do most of the steps

Meta wrote the SDK with agents in mind. Each SDK folder has an AGENTS.md for coding agents, and the ESP32 README says "Any agent that reads AGENTS.md can build and flash from this repository." Meta's own route is Muse Code: install it with curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | sh, then run muse --disable-sandbox in the esp32/ folder. The flag "lets it reach your board's USB serial port."

Your agent can plan the build first, too. hackshop's MCP server, at https://www.hackshop.dev/mcp or as the hackshop-mcp npm package, lets an agent pick a board for your goals and budget and fetch the parts list and flashing steps. It never buys anything without your OK.

What stays with you:

  • Plugging in the cable and pressing BOOT or RESET when asked.
  • Approving purchases and doing the checkout yourself.
  • Pairing in the Muse app under Settings > Devices with Developer mode on. Your gadget appears with a "MuseGadget" prefix.
  • Reading what the agent is about to run. --disable-sandbox gives it more access, so watch the commands.

A first hardware project for beginners, step by step

  1. Pick a board from the table above. Each one has a build page, such as the AIPI Lite build, with parts and steps.
  2. Order the board and a USB-C data cable.
  3. Get a Muse SDK token, which every gadget needs to pair, and install the Muse app.
  4. Let your agent install ESP-IDF 6.0.1, build and flash, or run the three commands yourself.
  5. Watch the status light or screen, then pair in the Muse app.

hackshop's build pages estimate one to three hours of setup for most of these boards. Plan an afternoon, and do not judge yourself by the first tool install.

One more shortcut: hackshop rates every board like a ski run. A green circle means Beginner, no tools: a USB-C data cable and one flash command. A blue square means Intermediate: an extra step such as a backup before flashing. A black diamond means Expert: it needs a pro, or you are better off buying something finished. Start with a green circle. You will see the rating on every board page.

Questions people ask

Do I need to solder for my first hardware project?

No. The boards Meta's Muse SDK supports are complete dev boards or finished devices. You connect them over USB, flash the firmware and pair them in the Muse app.

Can I use a Windows PC?

Meta's ESP32 SDK lists a computer running macOS or Linux as a requirement, so Windows is not on the supported path. A Raspberry Pi running the Linux SDK is another route.

Can I break my board by flashing it?

It can happen, which is why Meta's page warns about bricked boards. Many failed flashes are recoverable: hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT and flash again. Do not enable Secure Boot or flash encryption on a board you want to keep reflashing, and back up factory data on boards that need it.

How long does a first build take?

hackshop's build pages estimate one to three hours for most ESP32 boards. The flash itself takes seconds to a few minutes. Installing the tools and the first build take most of the time.

faq.q: How much does it cost to run a 3D printer?
faq.a: Very little per part with PLA. Filament runs about $16 to $25 per kg, so a 40 g part uses $0.64 to $1.00. Power is about $0.18 for a 10-hour print at around 100 W. A replacement nozzle (about $20) and build plate ($19.99 to about $37) add a little each year.

faq.q: What is the cheapest beginner 3D printer?
faq.a: In the prices checked for this guide, the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE ($199) and the Bambu Lab A1 mini ($219) were the lowest. The A1 mini's 180 mm build volume is plenty for gadget stands and small cases.

faq.q: Is it safe to 3D print at home?
faq.a: PLA generally emits fewer contaminants than ABS or nylon, according to UL Chemical Insights. UL still recommends ventilation that vents to the outside. Print PLA indoors and keep the room ventilated.

faq.q: Do I need a 3D printer to build an AI gadget?

bodyHtml:
Should you buy a 3D printer? Buy one if you will print more than a few dozen small parts a year, have a ventilated spot for it, and enjoy tinkering. If you need one or two parts, like a stand for a gadget, a library, makerspace or online service is cheaper. Beginner printers start around $200, and a small PLA part costs well under a dollar in filament and power.

Quick answer

A Bambu Lab A1 mini costs $219. Add a spare nozzle and build plate and the first year runs about $259 before filament. A 40 g PLA part costs about $0.67 to print at home, versus $4 to $8 at libraries that charge $0.10 to $0.20 per gram. So the printer pays for itself after roughly 36 to 78 parts a year. Below that, use a library or service. Run your own numbers in the 3D print cost calculator.

For gadget stands and small cases in PLA, any of these is enough. Enclosures matter more for ABS or ASA: Bambu does not recommend ABS, ASA, PC, PA or PET on the open-frame A1 mini.

Running costs: filament, power and wear parts

  • Filament. Bambu PLA Basic is $15.99 per 1 kg refill, $18.99 with a spool, and as low as $11.19 a roll for 10 or more. Prusa estimates PLA at about $25/kg. A 40 g part uses $0.64 to $1.00 of it.
  • Electricity. Bambu measured about 80 W for the A1 mini, 95 W for the A1 and 105 W for the P1S while printing PLA, and 4 to 7 W on standby. At the July 2026 US average of 18.31¢ per kWh, a 10-hour print at about 100 W costs about $0.18.
  • Wear parts. Prusa lists a replacement nozzle at about $20 (it "lasts hundreds of print hours") and a print sheet at about $37. Bambu's textured PEI plate starts at $19.99.
  • Add-ons. Multi-color units cost extra. Bambu's AMS 2 Pro is $269 on sale.

Prusa says most users spend $25 to $50 a month on filament. If you print a few stands a year, you will spend a few dollars.

Break-even: when owning beats a library or service

A worked example. Assumptions: an A1 mini at $219, plus a spare nozzle (about $20) and build plate ($19.99) in the first year, for about $259. Each part weighs 40 g and prints in about two hours at 80 W, so it costs about $0.64 in filament and $0.03 in power.

So the printer pays for itself at about 36 parts a year against a $0.20/g library, 49 against $0.15/g, and 78 against $0.10/g. Skip the spare nozzle and plate and those numbers drop to about 30, 42 and 66. Makerspace dues pass the cost of an A1 mini within a few months, but they also buy you every other tool and people who can help. Online services can be cheap for small parts, especially if you batch several into one order; the printer wins when you want to change a design and print it again the same day.

The learning curve

Getting started is the easy part. Bambu says the A1 mini comes pre-assembled and "only takes about 20 minutes to set up for your first print." The learning comes after: using a slicer, choosing supports and infill, getting the first layer to stick, and working out why a print failed. Expect some wasted filament in your first weeks. A kit like the $925 Prusa CORE One+ teaches you how the machine works, but takes longer before your first print.

Space, noise and fumes

A printer needs a stable surface and room around it. The A1 mini measures 347 × 315 × 365 mm and weighs 5.5 kg. The enclosed P1S is 389 × 389 × 458 mm and 12.95 kg. Prints run for hours, so put it where fan and motor noise will not keep anyone up.

Fumes depend on the material. UL Chemical Insights says PLA "generally emits fewer contaminants," while ABS and nylon "print at higher temperatures and consequently release significantly more UFPs and VOCs." UL recommends ventilation or local exhaust "that vents directly to the outside," and reports that ventilated enclosures cut particles by 99.7% and total VOCs by 69.5%. If the printer will live in a bedroom or small office, stick to PLA and keep the room ventilated.

So, should you buy a 3D printer?

Buy one if

  • You expect to print dozens of parts a year, or to revise a design several times in a day.
  • You have a ventilated spot where long prints will not bother anyone.
  • You enjoy the tinkering as much as the parts.

Wait if

  • You need one stand for an AI gadget. hackshop's printable stands, like the one on the M5Stack StickS3 build page, are small STL files any library or service can print.
  • You want ABS or nylon but have no ventilated space.
  • You would use it a few times and let it gather dust.

A makerspace is a good middle step. Learn on its printers, then buy your own if you keep going back.

Questions people ask

How much does it cost to run a 3D printer?

Very little per part with PLA. Filament runs about $16 to $25 per kg, so a 40 g part uses $0.64 to $1.00. Power is about $0.18 for a 10-hour print at around 100 W. A replacement nozzle (about $20) and build plate ($19.99 to about $37) add a little each year.

What is the cheapest beginner 3D printer?

In the prices checked for this guide, the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE ($199) and the Bambu Lab A1 mini ($219) were the lowest. The A1 mini's 180 mm build volume is plenty for gadget stands and small cases.

Is it safe to 3D print at home?

PLA generally emits fewer contaminants than ABS or nylon, according to UL Chemical Insights. UL still recommends ventilation that vents to the outside. Print PLA indoors and keep the room ventilated.

Do I need a 3D printer to build an AI gadget?

No. Stands are optional, and a library, makerspace or online service can print one for you. hackshop's build pages include stand files you can send to any of them.

bodyHtml:
You can get something 3D printed without a printer in three ways: upload a file to an online service, ask your public library, or join a makerspace. Online services like JLC3DP list FDM prints from $1.00 with a three-day build time, some libraries charge $0.10 to $0.20 per gram, and makerspace memberships run about $72 to $95 a month. All of them want a 3D model file, usually STL or 3MF.

Quick answer

For one small part, like a stand for an AI gadget, check your library first: it is local and priced by the gram. If it does not print for the public, compare quotes from an online service and batch several parts into one order. Join a makerspace if you want to print often and learn. hackshop's printable stands come as STL and STEP files on each board's build page, ready to send.

Online 3D printing services

You upload a file, pick a material and get a price. Starting prices are headlines. Your real cost depends on size, material and shipping.

  • JLC3DP. FDM from $1.00 (3 days), SLA resin from $0.30 (2 days) and MJF nylon from $1.00 (3 days). Tolerances run from ±0.2 mm (SLA) to ±0.3 mm (FDM). It accepts STL, STP, STEP, OBJ and 3MF, with walls over 1.2 mm and no part thinner than 0.8 mm.
  • Craftcloud. A marketplace from All3DP that compares quotes from "more than 150 professional services worldwide," with no minimum order and no registration required.
  • PCBWay. FDM in PLA, ABS, PC, PEEK, TPU and carbon-fiber-filled materials, ±0.2 mm tolerance under 100 mm, and a 1.5 mm minimum wall.
  • Xometry and Protolabs. Industrial services with instant quotes and parts in as little as one day. Xometry advertises free shipping on US orders. Protolabs says it has no minimum order quantities.
  • Treatstock. A multi-supplier platform with instant quotes, no minimum order and buyer protection.
  • Shapeways. It filed for Chapter 7 in July 2024, then reopened in August 2024 after a company formed by its original founders bought the assets. It now operates from Eindhoven and promotes "50+ high quality materials" and shipping to 130 countries.

Public libraries

Some public libraries print for patrons, often by the gram. Policies vary a lot. Real examples, checked October 5, 2026:

  • Austin Public Library (TX). Austin residents with a full access library card in good standing can request one free 3D print per month.
  • Arlington Public Library (TX). $0.20 per gram, calculated after the print finishes. STL files only, library filament only, and no weapons or replicas.
  • Brownsville Public Library (TX). $0.15 per gram for all colors and projects. Turnaround is 60 minutes to a few days.
  • Downers Grove Public Library (IL). $0.10 per gram with a $1.00 minimum. It can take up to three weeks. The maximum size is 350 × 320 × 325 mm, and the PLA is not food safe.

To find yours, search your library's website for "3D printing" or "maker." Before you send a file, ask what format they accept, whether they print for non-residents and how long the queue is.

Makerspaces, Fab Labs and school labs

A makerspace gives you printers and people who know them. hackerspaces.org describes hackerspaces as "community-operated physical places, where people share their interest in tinkering with technology, meet and work on their projects, and learn from each other."

  • Asmbly Makerspace (Austin). $95 a month base membership, with 3D printing, lasers, a woodshop, a metal shop and an electronics lab.
  • Dallas Makerspace. $72 a month for 2026, with 24/7 access and reduced rates for students, retirees, veterans and first responders.
  • Maker Nexus (Sunnyvale, CA). The $75 a month Limited membership includes the 3D printers and electronics lab.

How to find a local one

  • Nation of Makers keeps a crowdsourced map of US maker organizations, including makerspaces, hackerspaces and Fab Labs in libraries, museums and schools.
  • fablabs.io is the Fab Foundation's official Fab Lab directory. Its data feed has 319 US listings, some planned or closed, so call before you go.
  • Your school. UT Austin's Hello Maker Studio is free for UT students, filament included. Arapahoe Community College's library in Colorado lets students, staff and instructors use its 3D printer for free.

What file to send, and how to get it right

  • STL is the safe choice. Some libraries, like Arlington, take STL only.
  • 3MF carries the shape plus extras like units. JLC3DP accepts it.
  • STEP (or STP) is an exact CAD format that keeps true curves. JLC3DP accepts it too.

Before you upload:

  1. Check the units. A part modeled in millimeters but read as inches comes out 25.4 times too big.
  2. Check wall thickness. JLC3DP wants walls over 1.2 mm; PCBWay's FDM minimum is 1.5 mm.
  3. Leave clearance where parts fit together. With tolerances of ±0.2 to ±0.3 mm, a pocket for a device should be a little larger than the device.
  4. Choose PLA for indoor stands and cases unless you need heat resistance or flex.
  5. Order one copy first, check the fit, then order more.

If you are building an AI gadget, you may not need to model anything. hackshop's build pages include printable desk stands, as STL and STEP files, for the M5Stack StickS3, the M5Stack StickC Plus2, the Waveshare round AMOLED and the Waveshare ESP32-C6 1.8-inch AMOLED. Each stand is shaped for its board, so you can send the file as-is.

Turnaround and ordering tips

  • Count build time plus shipping. JLC3DP's FDM build time is three days before shipping. Craftcloud says orders ship in 24 to 48 hours.
  • Expect library times to vary. Brownsville quotes 60 minutes to a few days; Downers Grove says up to three weeks.
  • Batch your parts. Several parts in one order can share one shipping charge.
  • Compare quotes. Marketplaces like Craftcloud and Treatstock show several suppliers at once.
  • Know the rules. Libraries limit size, material and content.
